Conclude that any backtesting result is only meaningful, and any add-on or model disallowance defensible, when tied to a properly calibrated VaR measure as defined in the standard.

clause_a.excerpt: Backtesting requirements compare the value-at-risk (VaR) measure calibrated to a one-day holding period against each of the actual P&L (APL) and hypothetical P&L (HPL)

clause_b.excerpt: Value at risk (VaR): A measure of the worst expected loss on a portfolio of instruments resulting from market movements over a given time horizon and a pre-defined confidence level.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_backtesting||.why: When adjudicating whether a backtesting exception can be legitimately disregarded, check the modellability status of the risk factor driving it: the standard permits an exception to be set aside only where it is driven by a non-modellable risk factor (NMRF) that receives an SES capital requirement exceeding the day's loss, and only with SAMA notification and supporting documentation. Risk factor modellability (RFET and the [11.25]–[11.26] principles) is what determines whether a factor is an NMRF in the first place, so the two concepts are directly linked in the exception-treatment test. Conclude that a bank cannot claim the disregard relief without first establishing, to SAMA's satisfaction, that the factor is genuinely non-modellable and separately capitalised at the required desk level.

clause_a.excerpt: If the backtesting exception at a desk-level test is being driven by a non-modellable risk factor that receives an SES capital requirement... it is permitted to be disregarded

clause_b.excerpt: the risk factor must be excluded from the ES model and subject to capital requirements as an NMRF

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_hpl||markdown.why: When reviewing PLA test compliance, understand that HPL is one of the two inputs the test compares — the PLA test assesses correlation and distributional similarity between the risk-theoretical P&L (RTPL) and the HPL. This drives concrete constraints: banks must not align HPL input data with RTPL input data, adjustments for 'residual operational noise' are prohibited, and any permitted RTPL input alignments must be documented and justified to SAMA. Conclude that the integrity of HPL construction (excluding intraday trades, fees, and non-daily valuation adjustments as specified) directly determines whether PLA results are valid, so a reviewer must scrutinise HPL scope before relying on the test outcome.

clause_a.excerpt: Banks are not permitted to align HPL input data for risk factors with input data used in RTPL.

clause_b.excerpt: the Spearman correlation metric to assess the correlation between RTPL and HPL; and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test metric to assess similarity of the distributions of RTPL and HPL

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_internal_mode.why: When scoping the ongoing conditions for a bank to retain IMA capital treatment, treat the PLA test as an embedded IMA requirement rather than an independent measure: the IMA mandates that the independent risk control unit conduct regular PLA assessments at the trading desk level, and the standard requires the PLA test programme to begin when the internal models capital requirement becomes effective and to be reported for SAMA model approval. PLA results, alongside backtesting and the RFET, feed quarterly into which desks remain eligible for the IMA. Conclude that a compliance reviewer evaluating continued IMA approval should confirm PLA testing is running per the standard, since desk-level PLA failure affects whether that desk stays within the internal-models regime.

clause_a.excerpt: The bank's risk control unit must conduct regular backtesting and PLA assessments at the trading desk level.

clause_b.excerpt: The implementation of the backtesting programme and the PLA test must begin on the date that the internal models capital requirement becomes effective.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_ks_metric||ma.why: When assessing whether a trading desk retains eligibility for the Internal Models Approach (IMA), treat the KS test metric as one of the two hard thresholds that determine the PLA test outcome, not as a standalone concept. Under this SAMA market-risk framework, the PLA test allocates a desk to green, amber or red zones, and para 12.42 makes the KS distributional metric a gating input (green requires KS below 0.09; red if KS above 0.12). Consequently, a compliance reviewer confirming IMA eligibility must verify the KS metric against these numeric bounds because a red-zone KS result forces the desk onto the standardised approach until it re-qualifies.

clause_a.excerpt: The KS test metric is the largest absolute difference observed between these two empirical cumulative distribution functions at any P&L value.

clause_b.excerpt: a trading desk is allocated to a PLA test red zone, an amber zone or a green zone... the KS distributional test metric is below 0.09

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_pla_test||mar.why: When scoping what data a desk must produce to pass the PLA test, understand that RTPL is one of the two P&L series the test compares — the PLA test has no meaning without it. Para 12.34–12.35 require the test metrics to be computed from the most recent 250 trading days of RTPL and HPL observations, and paras 12.30–12.33 constrain how RTPL input data may or may not be adjusted. A reviewer confirming PLA compliance should therefore check both the integrity of the RTPL series and that any RTPL input-data alignment was documented and notified to SAMA, since improper RTPL adjustments directly distort the test result.

clause_a.excerpt: The PLA requirements are based on two test metrics... to assess the correlation between RTPL and HPL

clause_b.excerpt: the bank must use the time series of the most recent 250 trading days of observations of RTPL and HPL

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_pla_test||mar.why: When evaluating PLA test eligibility, treat the Spearman correlation metric as the second mandatory gating input alongside the KS metric — a desk cannot reach the green zone without meeting the correlation threshold. Para 12.34 establishes the Spearman metric as one of the two PLA requirements (assessing correlation between RTPL and HPL), and para 12.42 makes correlation above 0.80 a green-zone condition and below 0.7 a red-zone trigger. A compliance reviewer confirming IMA eligibility must verify the Spearman result against these bounds, because a weak correlation alone can push a desk to the standardised approach.

clause_a.excerpt: the Spearman correlation metric to assess the correlation between RTPL and HPL

clause_b.excerpt: Banks must calculate the Spearman correlation coefficient of the two time series of rank values

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_rtpl||markdow.why: When verifying how the Spearman metric is computed, note that RTPL supplies one of the two rank-ordered P&L series it operates on, so RTPL data quality directly drives the correlation result. Para 12.37 requires banks to rank the RTPL time series by size, and para 12.38 computes the Spearman coefficient of the RTPL and HPL rank series; para 12.33 further bars aligning RTPL and HPL inputs to reduce operational noise. A reviewer should therefore confirm the RTPL series is properly constructed and unadjusted before relying on the resulting Spearman metric for PLA zone allocation.

clause_a.excerpt: for a time series of RTPL, banks must produce a corresponding time series of ranks based on size

clause_b.excerpt: Banks must calculate the Spearman correlation coefficient of the two time series of rank values of RTPL and HPL

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_hpl||markdown.why: When verifying the Spearman metric, recognise that HPL is the second P&L series it ranks and correlates against RTPL, so HPL construction rules (paras 12.25–12.28: exclude intraday trades, fees, certain valuation adjustments) feed directly into the metric's validity. Para 12.36 requires ranking the HPL time series, and para 12.38 computes the correlation of the RTPL and HPL rank series; para 12.33 prohibits aligning HPL inputs with RTPL to mask noise. A reviewer confirming PLA compliance should check that HPL was compiled per the defined exclusions before treating the Spearman result as reliable for zone allocation.

clause_a.excerpt: For a time series of HPL, banks must produce a corresponding time series of ranks based on the size of the P&L

clause_b.excerpt: the Spearman correlation metric to assess the correlation between RTPL and HPL

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_drc_model||ma.why: When assessing a bank's internal models approach (IMA) for market risk capital under this SAMA framework, treat Default Risk Charge (DRC) modelling and Value-at-Risk as distinct but co-resident components of the same IMA capital calculation, not interchangeable measures. VaR is defined in the glossary as a measure of worst expected loss over a horizon at a confidence level, whereas the DRC internal model captures jump-to-default losses not reflected in ordinary price-movement measures; both feed the IMA capital requirement subject to the validation, backtesting and independent risk-control obligations in [10]. Consequently, verify that a bank approved for IMA runs and validates each measure on its own terms — you cannot infer DRC adequacy from VaR/backtesting results, and each must independently satisfy SAMA's model-validation and governance requirements.

clause_a.excerpt: A distinct unit of the bank... must conduct the initial and ongoing validation of all internal models used to determine market risk capital requirements.

clause_b.excerpt: Value at risk (VaR): A measure of the worst expected loss on a portfolio of instruments resulting from market movements over a given time horizon and a pre-defined confidence level.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_commodities_r.why: When determining capital charges for a bank eligible to use the simplified standardised approach, treat commodities risk as one of the four risk categories that the approach expressly covers and measures with prescribed, fixed percentages rather than sensitivity-based methods. Paragraph 14.1(1) scopes [14.3]–[14.73] to interest rate, equity, FX and commodities risk, and 14.72–14.73 set the concrete charges (15% of net position plus 3% of gross positions) for commodities. So for an eligible bank (non–G-SIB/D-SIB, no IMA, no correlation trading), you would calculate commodities capital using these flat charges and sum them arithmetically per 14.1(3) — but confirm SAMA has not mandated the full standardised approach for sizeable commodity risk under 3.9(2).

clause_a.excerpt: The capital requirement will equal 15% of the net position, long or short, in each commodity.

clause_b.excerpt: [14.3] to [14.73] deal with interest rate, equity, foreign exchange (FX) and commodities risk.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_equity_risk||.why: When scoping the simplified standardised approach for an eligible bank, equity risk is one of the four defined categories the approach measures, and its charge is computed separately and summed with the others rather than netted across risk classes. Paragraph 14.1(1) lists equity risk within [14.3]–[14.73], and 14.75 confirms equities capital numbers are added to the relevant category totals with general and specific market risk incorporated. Conclude that equity positions of an eligible bank must be capitalised under the simplified rules and arithmetically aggregated per 14.1(3); do not assume any diversification offset between equity and other risk classes under this approach.

clause_a.excerpt: The capital requirement under the simplified standardised approach will be the measures of risk obtained from [14.2] to [14.86], summed arithmetically.

clause_b.excerpt: [14.3] to [14.73] deal with interest rate, equity, foreign exchange (FX) and commodities risk.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_interest_rate.why: When applying the simplified standardised approach for an eligible bank, interest rate risk is the first of the four defined risk categories covered, and the framework also treats interest rate risk as a component within commodities and options measurement rather than only a standalone book. Paragraph 14.1(1) scopes interest rate risk into [14.3]–[14.73], while 14.73 adds a 3% gross-position charge to protect against basis, interest rate and forward gap risk in commodities. Accordingly, capitalise a bank's interest rate positions under the simplified rules and check that interest rate elements embedded in forward/derivative positions (e.g. commodities carry) are captured through the additional charges, not omitted.

clause_a.excerpt: [14.3] to [14.73] deal with interest rate, equity, foreign exchange (FX) and commodities risk.

clause_b.excerpt: to protect the bank against basis risk, interest rate risk and forward gap risk under the simplified approach... an additional capital requirement equivalent to 3% of the bank's gross positions.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_general_marke.why: When distinguishing risk types for market risk capital, understand that general market risk is a cross-cutting component (broad market-wide price movement) that applies to interest-rate instruments alongside specific risk, and interest rate risk is one of the defined risk classes to which it attaches. The glossary anchors 'general interest rate risk' as a listed risk class, and the simplified-approach text (14.75) confirms option carve-outs generate capital incorporating 'both general market risk and specific risk' added back to the interest-rate category. For a capital calculation you would therefore treat general market risk and interest rate risk as related layers — general market risk is measured within the interest-rate class, not as a substitute for it — and ensure both the general and specific components are captured for interest-rate positions.

clause_a.excerpt: subject to separately calculated capital requirements that incorporate both general market risk and specific risk.

clause_b.excerpt: Risk class: A defined list of risks... general interest rate risk, credit spread risk (non-securitisation)... FX risk, equity risk and commodity risk.

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_interest_rate.why: When scoping market-risk capital charges under this SAMA framework, treat general interest rate risk and specific risk as two distinct components that must be capitalised separately, not merged. The framework's defined 'Risk class' list separates general interest rate risk from credit spread (specific) risk, and worked provisions (e.g. first-to-default credit derivative treatment) compute specific-risk charges independently of general rate movements. Conclude that an interest-rate instrument's capital requirement will draw on both risk categories, and verify which chapter/section governs each rather than assuming one charge covers both.

clause_a.excerpt: a bond ... has risk positions in general interest rate risk, credit spread risk (non-securitisation) and FX risk

clause_b.excerpt: Risk class: ... general interest rate risk, credit spread risk (non-securitisation) ... FX risk, equity risk and commodity risk

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_equity_risk||.why: When computing the equity charge under the standardised approaches, understand that equity risk is one of the defined risk classes that feeds the overall general market risk measurement, and that under the simplified standardised approach equity, interest rate, FX and commodities charges are summed arithmetically. The framework lists equity risk within the enumerated risk classes and directs that these component risk measures be aggregated for the capital requirement. Conclude that the equity charge is not standalone but part of the summed general market risk total, and check [14.1]–[14.73] for the applicable equity computation.

clause_a.excerpt: [14.3] to [14.73] deal with interest rate, equity, foreign exchange (FX) and commodities risk

clause_b.excerpt: the measures of risk obtained ... summed arithmetically

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_equity_risk||.why: When capitalising an equity position, note that the framework treats equity risk as one of the defined risk classes and, consistent with the standardised structure, separates specific (issuer-level) risk from general market risk. The 'Risk class' definition enumerates equity risk alongside credit spread (specific) risk, and the standardised approach requires distinct component measures to be summed. Conclude that an equity holding may attract both a specific-risk and a general-risk element, and verify the equity chapter for how each is derived rather than applying a single blended charge.

clause_a.excerpt: Risk class: ... FX risk, equity risk and commodity risk

clause_b.excerpt: The capital requirement for specific risk for a first-to-default credit derivative is the lesser of ...

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_credit_risk_f.why: When determining specific-risk capital for credit derivatives, this document itself sets out the specific-risk charges and offsets for reference credit instruments, so specific risk here is a market-risk (trading-book) concept computed within these minimum capital requirements. The provisions on first-to-default and nth-to-default derivatives prescribe the specific-risk charge as the lesser of aggregated component charges or the maximum credit event payment. Conclude that these specific-risk rules govern trading-book credit-derivative positions; do not conflate them with the separate credit-risk (banking-book) capital framework without confirming which book the position sits in.

clause_a.excerpt: The capital requirement for specific risk for a first-to-default credit derivative is the lesser of: (a) the sum of the specific risk capital requirements ...; and (b) the maximum possible credit event payment

clause_b.excerpt: the bank is allowed to reduce ... both the capital requirement for specific risk for the reference credit instrument and that part of the capital requirement for specific risk for the credit derivative

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_duration_meth.why: When electing a method to measure general market risk for interest-rate positions, note that the duration method is an alternative, more granular measurement of general market risk that requires SAMA's consent and must be used continuously once adopted. The provision expressly frames the duration method as a way to measure 'all of their general market risk' by calculating each position's price sensitivity separately, subject to SAMA monitoring. Conclude that using the duration method is not a free choice: it needs prior SAMA approval, binds the bank to consistent application, and any switch back requires further SAMA approval.

clause_a.excerpt: banks with the necessary capability may, with SAMA' consent, use a more accurate method of measuring all of their general market risk by calculating the price sensitivity of each position separately

clause_b.excerpt: Banks must elect and use the method on a continuous basis (unless a change in method is approved by SAMA)

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_general_marke.why: When determining a bank's market risk capital charge for interest-rate and options positions under the simplified standardised approach, do not treat general market risk and the maturity method as independent inputs — the maturity method is one of the mechanics through which the general market risk charge is measured. The same instrument (SAMA_EN_3553) links them by requiring delta-weighted and derivative positions to be slotted into maturity time bands (with sub-three-month positions floored at a three-month weighting) before the general market risk charge is applied. Conclude that any assessment of the general market risk requirement for these positions must confirm correct maturity treatment, since the maturity determination feeds directly into the capital number.

clause_a.excerpt: all Banks (D-SIBs and Non D-SIBs) are required to calculate the market risk capital charge by using the Standardised Approach

clause_b.excerpt: the maturity of the derivative contract is considered in determining the offsetting criterion, not the maturity of the underlying instrument

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_delta_plus_me.why: When establishing which options capital methodology a bank may use, treat the delta-plus method as a component within the simplified approach for options, not as a standalone alternative regime — the delta-plus method is one of the permissible methods offered under the simplified standardised approach at SAMA's discretion. The instrument (SAMA_EN_3553) states that banks solely holding purchased options may use the basic simplified treatment, while banks that write options are expected to use the delta-plus method or scenario approach. Conclude that eligibility turns on whether the bank writes options; a written-option book cannot rely on the basic simplified treatment and must apply delta-plus (with gamma and vega add-ons) or the scenario approach.

clause_a.excerpt: the delta-equivalent position of each option becomes part of the simplified standardised approach set out in [14.3] to [14.73]

clause_b.excerpt: Those banks which also write options are expected to use the delta-plus method or scenario app[roach]

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_delta_plus_me.why: When applying the delta-plus method, do not treat delta capture as sufficient — the same instrument requires that gamma and vega risks be separately measured and charged on top of the delta-equivalent position. SAMA_EN_3553 states delta does not sufficiently cover options risk, so banks writing options must additionally measure gamma and vega to arrive at the total capital requirement. Conclude that a delta-plus capital calculation is incomplete unless the separate gamma (and vega) capital requirements are also computed and added.

clause_a.excerpt: Separate capital requirements are then applied to the gamma and vega risks of the option positions

clause_b.excerpt: since delta does not sufficiently cover the risks associated with options positions, banks will also be required to measure gamma ... and vega ... sensitivities

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_delta_plus_me.why: When a bank writes options, understand delta-plus and the scenario approach as the two alternative methods offered for the same purpose under the simplified standardised approach — a bank chooses one, not both. The same instrument (SAMA_EN_3553) presents them together: delta-plus uses Greek-letter sensitivities while the scenario approach uses simulation over a scenario grid, and for both the specific risk charge is derived by applying specific risk weights to the delta-equivalent. Conclude that a compliance review should confirm which single method the bank has adopted for its written-option positions and that the associated (gamma/vega or scenario-grid) computations are consistent with the chosen method.

clause_a.excerpt: The delta-plus method uses the sensitivity parameters or Greek letters associated with options to measure their market risk

clause_b.excerpt: The scenario approach uses simulation techniques ... the general market risk charge is determined by the scenario grid ... that produces the largest loss

markdown_sama_en_3553_ver1_internal_mode.why: When assessing whether a bank can use the internal models approach (IMA) for a given position, treat risk factor modellability as a gating precondition rather than a technical detail — under the same instrument (SAMA_EN_3553), a risk factor that fails the modellability principles must be excluded from the ES model and capitalised as a non-modellable risk factor (NMRF). SAMA may deem data unsuitable for a particular risk factor and force NMRF treatment, and modellability is judged against defined principles, not merely the count of real-price observations. Conclude that IMA capital recognition cannot be assumed for the full portfolio; you must check which risk factors pass the RFET/modellability principles and confirm that non-modellable ones carry the separate NMRF charge.

clause_a.excerpt: a distinct unit ... must conduct the initial and ongoing validation of all internal models used to determine market risk capital requirements

clause_b.excerpt: the risk factor must be excluded from the ES model and subject to capital requirements as an NMRF

markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_ews||markdown.why: When assessing a bank's problem-loan controls under these Guidelines, treat the watch list as the operational output of the EWS process, not a standalone register: the EWS unit interprets signals and decides which borrowers go onto the watch list for corrective action. The link tells you that a compliant EWS framework must feed a properly maintained watch list, with risk-management approval to remove loans and defined maximum tenure before escalation. Check that inclusion criteria, minimum data fields, and monthly reporting to a management committee/Board are documented, since SAMA treats an effective EWS framework as a 'mandatory requirement.'

clause_a.excerpt: determine whether that borrower should be included in the watch list (prepared on the basis of EWS) for further corrective action

clause_b.excerpt: A loan is added to the watch list prepared on the basis of EWS ... Risk management approval required to remove the loan from watch list

markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_ews||markdown.why: When evaluating whether a bank's NPL lifecycle is coherent, connect early identification (EWS) to the restructuring/monitoring stage: the Guidelines state that effective early identification and early restructuring can prevent long-term default and losses. This link tells you the two functions are ends of one continuum — EWS triggers should ultimately support timely restructuring where a borrower is viable and cooperative. clause_a.excerpt: To allow the opportunity to develop a corrective action plan at a very early stage

clause_b.excerpt: If banks are effective in identifying early warning signs ... engaging in early restructuring solutions, this could prevent long-term default and losses

markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_ews||markdown.caveat: The two nodes are thematically joined within the same Guidelines rather than by a direct article-level cross-reference; confirm the intended escalation path in the primary text.

markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_watch_list||m.why: When reviewing escalation controls, read the watch list and Workout Unit as sequential stages of the same mandatory pathway: a loan may remain on the watch list only temporarily, and once the bank's specified time expires it must be either returned to the originating unit (if resolved) or transferred to the Workout Unit. The Guidelines require a documented, time-bound policy with clear criteria and approvals for the mandatory transfer to the WU. Check that the bank has defined the maximum watch-list tenure and the objective transfer triggers, because leaving stressed loans in the originating unit is expressly flagged as raising NPLs and lowering recovery.

clause_a.excerpt: After that period, loan must be either returned to originating unit or transferred to Workout Unit

clause_b.excerpt: Banks shall establish and document a policy with clear and objective time-bound criteria for the mandatory transfer of loans ... to the Workout Unit

markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_llcr||markdow.why: When assessing how a bank decides whether to restructure a distressed loan, note that the LLCR is the analytical tool assigned to Workout teams for viability assessment of medium- to long-term and project-finance debt. markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_workout_plan|.why: When mapping who is accountable for a restructuring outcome, treat the workout plan as the product the Workout Unit is required to design and negotiate: the WU tailors the restructuring option to the borrower, and the bank may only approve a plan where projected cash flows suffice and the borrower is cooperative. markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_npl_strategy|.why: When assessing a bank's compliance with SAMA's Guidelines on Management of Problem Loans, treat portfolio segmentation as an operative component of the NPL strategy rather than a separate exercise: the design phase requires targets set 'by main portfolios', and segmentation is the mechanism that produces those homogeneous portfolios. clause_b.excerpt: It is the essential first step in developing a cost-effective and efficient approach to NPL resolution.

markdown_sama_en_3575_ver1_financial_via.why: When testing whether a workout plan rests on sound footing, treat the financial viability analysis (ratios, balance-sheet review, cash-flow analysis) as the quantitative basis for the plan's core pre-condition. markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_cash_inflows|.why: When computing the LCR denominator, treat Cash Inflows and Total Net Cash Outflows as a single linked calculation, not independent figures, because the standard defines net outflows precisely as outflows minus inflows and caps recognised inflows at 75% of total expected outflows. The formula (outflows minus the lesser of inflows or 75% of outflows) means excess inflows cannot fully offset outflows, and the no-double-counting rule bars counting an HQLA-included asset's inflows again. Conclude that inflow recognition is bounded by this 75% cap and the anti-double-counting constraint, so a bank cannot reduce its net outflow figure below 25% of gross outflows through inflows alone.

clause_a.excerpt: Derivatives cash inflows: the sum of all net cash inflows should receive a 100% inflow factor

clause_b.excerpt: total expected cash inflows ... up to an aggregate cap of 75% of total expected cash outflows

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_cash_outflows.why: When computing the LCR denominator for a SAMA-supervised bank, treat 'Cash Outflows' as a component of, not a synonym for, 'Total Net Cash Outflows': the net figure is total expected outflows minus capped inflows over the 30-day stress horizon. Paragraph 69 defines the net measure and its inflow cap at 75% of total expected outflows, so gross outflow categories feed directly into it. You should conclude that any outflow category (retail, wholesale, secured, derivatives) must be aggregated and then netted against eligible inflows, subject to the 75% floor on inflow offset, before assessing LCR compliance.

clause_a.excerpt: Total expected cash outflows are calculated by multiplying the outstanding balances of various categories or types of liabilities and off-balance sheet commitments by the rates at which they are expected to run off

clause_b.excerpt: total net cash outflows... is defined as the total expected cash outflows minus total expected cash inflows in the specified stress scenario for the subsequent 30 calendar days

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_cash_outflows.why: When building the outflow side of the LCR, retail deposit run-off is one of the specific categories whose balances are multiplied by prescribed run-off rates to produce total expected cash outflows. The standard sets differentiated rates — 3%/5% for stable insured deposits, minimum 10% and higher for less stable buckets — and lets supervisors add jurisdiction-specific buckets. You should therefore verify how SAMA has set the national retail run-off parameters (transparent and publicly available per para 70) and default deposits to 'less stable' buckets where stability criteria cannot be evidenced.

clause_a.excerpt: Total expected cash outflows are calculated by multiplying the outstanding balances of various categories or types of liabilities and off-balance sheet commitments by the rates at which they are expected to run off

clause_b.excerpt: Supervisory authorities are expected to develop additional buckets with higher run-off rates... with a minimum run-off rate of 10%

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_cash_outflows.why: Secured funding run-off is another prescribed outflow category feeding the total expected cash outflows in the LCR. For secured funding transactions maturing within 30 days, the outflow is calculated on the amount of funds raised (not collateral value), with factors driven by the quality of the underlying collateral — notably 0% against Level 1 assets. You should conclude that repo, reverse-repo, collateral swaps and customer short positions must be mapped to the relevant collateral-based factor, and not double-counted with other outflow categories.

clause_a.excerpt: Total expected cash outflows are calculated by multiplying the outstanding balances of various categories or types of liabilities and off-balance sheet commitments by the rates at which they are expected to run off

clause_b.excerpt: The amount of outflow is calculated based on the amount of funds raised through the transaction, and not the value of the underlying collateral

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_cash_outflows.why: Unsecured wholesale funding run-off is a defined outflow category contributing to total expected cash outflows, with run-off factors that turn on the counterparty type and operational relationship (e.g. 40%, reduced to 20% if fully insured, and 100% for other legal-entity customers). Note the definition captures liabilities from non-natural persons callable within 30 days, expressly excluding derivative obligations. You should classify each funding source by counterparty and operational status to apply the correct factor, and check that debt securities are only re-categorised as retail where the stated distribution limitations are met.

clause_a.excerpt: Total expected cash outflows are calculated by multiplying the outstanding balances of various categories or types of liabilities and off-balance sheet commitments by the rates at which they are expected to run off

clause_b.excerpt: 'unsecured wholesale funding' is defined as those liabilities and general obligations that are raised from non-natural persons... Obligations related to derivative contracts are explicitly excluded

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_maturity_mism.why: This link appears to connect the contractual maturity mismatch monitoring tool with the Basel Committee's 'Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision', and the text supports that connection: the LCR standard states it must be supplemented by supervisory assessment 'in line with the Sound Principles' and by the Part 2 monitoring tools, of which maturity mismatch is the first. Practically, you should not treat LCR compliance as sufficient on its own — the mismatch metric feeds a broader supervisory judgement under the Sound Principles, and supervisors may impose more stringent parameters based on that assessment. Verify how SAMA operationalises the Sound Principles alongside the monitoring tools before relying on LCR figures alone.

clause_a.excerpt: Examples of actions that supervisors can take are outlined in the Committee's Sound Principles (paragraphs 141-143)... I. Contractual maturity mismatch

clause_b.excerpt: the LCR... must be supplemented by detailed supervisory assessments of other aspects of the bank's liquidity risk management framework in line with the Sound Principles

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_maturity_mism.caveat: Relation is INFERRED/conceptual; the mismatch tool and Sound Principles are linked as parts of one framework rather than by a direct cross-reference between them — confirm in the primary text.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala||markdown.why: When assessing whether a bank may rely on committed liquidity facilities to plug an HQLA shortfall, treat ALA Option 1 as one of three specific alternative treatments authorised only within the general ALA regime, not as a free-standing entitlement. The ALA guidance sets overarching preconditions — usage capped at actual HQLA shortfall, ongoing reporting to the supervisor, and (for Option 1) typically central bank approval of the committed facility — that constrain any use of this option. You would therefore verify that both the ALA general rules and Option 1's specific conditions are satisfied before treating committed facility capacity as LCR-eligible.

clause_a.excerpt: use of Option 1 will typically require central bank approval of the committed facility.

clause_b.excerpt: A jurisdiction which intends to adopt one or more of the options for alternative treatment must be capable of limiting the uncertainty of performance

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala||markdown.why: When a bank faces a shortfall of domestic-currency HQLA, ALA Option 2 permits holding foreign-currency HQLA instead, but only as a subordinate option within the ALA framework and subject to that framework's usage cap and reporting duties. Option 2 adds its own conditions: currency mismatch positions must be justifiable, controlled within supervisor-agreed limits, and confined to freely and reliably convertible currencies, with foreign-exchange haircuts applied. You would conclude that eligibility turns on both the general ALA constraints and Option 2's currency-specific limits, and would check the supervisor's agreed mismatch limits before relying on foreign-currency HQLA.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank should not use an alternative treatment to meet its LCR more than its actual need as reflected by the shortfall of eligible HQLA

clause_b.excerpt: Option 2 would allow supervisors to permit banks that evidence a shortfall of HQLA in the domestic currency ... to hold HQLA in a currency that does not match

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala||markdown.why: When considering whether a bank can hold Level 2A assets beyond the 40% cap, treat ALA Option 3 as the third alternative treatment governed by the same ALA general rules (usage limited to actual shortfall, supervisory reporting), plus its own quality and haircut conditions. Option 3 requires the additional Level 2A assets to be of quality comparable to Level 1, subject to a minimum 20% haircut (5% above the standard 15%), while Level 2B assets stay within the 15% cap. You would conclude that exceeding the 40% cap is permissible only where both the overarching ALA limits and Option 3's higher qualifying standards are met.

clause_a.excerpt: The usage of any of the above options would be constrained by a limit specified by supervisors

clause_b.excerpt: the jurisdiction must only allow Level 2 assets that are of a quality (credit and liquidity) comparable to that for Level 1 assets

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_operational_d.why: When classifying corporate or institutional deposits for LCR run-off purposes, do not treat 'operational deposits' and 'unsecured wholesale funding run-off' as separate silos: operational deposits are a preferential carve-out within the unsecured wholesale funding regime, attracting the 25% factor only for the portion proven to serve clearing, custody or cash-management needs. Any excess balance falls back into the ordinary non-operational wholesale categories (e.g. 40% or 100% run-off), and if the bank cannot isolate the operational portion the entire deposit is treated as non-operational. You would therefore verify the operational-need methodology before applying the favourable factor, defaulting to the higher wholesale run-off rate where it is not demonstrable.

clause_a.excerpt: only that part of the deposit balance ... proven to serve a customer's operational needs can qualify as stable. Excess balances should be treated in the appropriate category for non-operational deposits

clause_b.excerpt: deposits and other funding from other institutions ... not specifically held for operational purposes ... The run-off factor for these funds is 100%.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_funding_conce.why: When determining a bank's LCR-related reporting obligations, recognise that 'Concentration of Funding' is not a standalone requirement but one of the Part 2 monitoring-tool metrics that sit alongside — and are distinct in status from — the binding LCR standard in Part 1. As a monitoring metric it defines specific thresholds (a significant counterparty/product exceeding 1% of the balance sheet; a significant currency being 5% or more of total liabilities) that supervisors use to detect negative trends, rather than a pass/fail ratio. You would conclude that funding-concentration figures are supervisory-monitoring inputs, and check the defined significance thresholds when scoping what must be reported under the monitoring-tools regime.

clause_a.excerpt: identify those sources of wholesale funding ... withdrawal of this funding could trigger liquidity problems ... more than 1% of the bank's total balance sheet

clause_b.excerpt: In addition to the LCR outlined in Part 1 to be used as a standard, this section outlines metrics to be used as consistent monitoring tools.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_lcr_by_curren.why: When determining what liquidity reporting a bank owes SAMA beyond the headline LCR, treat 'LCR by significant currency' as one of the five prescribed Part 2 monitoring metrics rather than an optional analysis. The parent document lists it explicitly (item IV) among the consistent monitoring tools that complement the single-currency LCR standard, so a bank must monitor and report foreign-currency LCR alongside the standard where SAMA applies these tools. Conclude that meeting the 100% LCR in one currency does not discharge the currency-mismatch monitoring obligation; check the foreign-currency LCR calculation (HQLA per currency / net outflows per currency, net of FX hedges) separately.

clause_a.excerpt: in order to better capture potential currency mismatches, banks and supervisors should also monitor the LCR in significant currencies

clause_b.excerpt: The metrics discussed in this section include the following: ... IV. LCR by significant currency

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_market_monito.why: When mapping the full set of liquidity-monitoring obligations, recognise that market-related monitoring tools are the fifth prescribed metric within the same Part 2 framework, not a distinct regime. Paragraph 176 lists them (item V) as a cornerstone metric supervisors use to assess a bank's liquidity risk, drawing on high-frequency market, financial-sector and bank-specific data as early-warning indicators. Conclude that this metric supplements the maturity-mismatch, funding-concentration, unencumbered-asset and currency metrics; do not treat market-data monitoring as external to the LCR supervisory package.

clause_a.excerpt: High frequency market data with little or no time lag can be used as early warning indicators in monitoring potential liquidity difficulties at banks.

clause_b.excerpt: The metrics discussed in this section include the following: ... V. Market-related monitoring tools

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_maturity_mism.why: When identifying reporting obligations under Part 2, treat contractual maturity mismatch as the first of the five prescribed monitoring metrics, carrying specific data assumptions that a bank cannot restate at its discretion. Paragraph 176 lists it (item I), and paragraphs 179–183 fix the assumptions — no rollover of liabilities, no new asset contracts, separate reporting of open-maturity instruments, contingent liabilities and rehypothecated collateral. Conclude that the mismatch report must follow these prescribed contractual assumptions and at minimum cover the LCR categories; verify open-maturity and contingent-trigger items are reported separately.

clause_a.excerpt: The contractual maturity mismatch profile identifies the gaps between the contractual inflows and outflows of liquidity for defined time bands.

clause_b.excerpt: The metrics discussed in this section include the following: I. Contractual maturity mismatch

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_monitoring_to.why: When scoping what a bank must report on assets it could mobilise for additional liquidity, treat 'available unencumbered assets' as the third prescribed Part 2 metric with defined reporting content, not a general risk-appetite disclosure. Paragraph 176 lists it (item III), and paragraphs 201–204 require reporting the amount, type and location of assets marketable as secondary-market collateral or eligible for central-bank standing facilities, plus re-pledgeable customer collateral. Conclude that only assets for which operational monetisation procedures are already in place count, and standing-facility eligibility excludes emergency assistance; check both conditions before reporting an asset as available.

clause_a.excerpt: The metrics discussed in this section include the following: ... III. Available unencumbered assets

clause_b.excerpt: These metrics provide supervisors with data on the quantity and key characteristics, including currency denomination and location, of banks' available unencumbered assets.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala_options||.why: When assessing the standing of the ALA guidance in Annex 3, understand that these options exist within a Basel Committee framework and that jurisdictional eligibility is externally validated, not self-declared. The document ties ALA use to Basel Committee oversight — notification of transition plans, self-assessment of eligibility, and an independent peer review conducted as part of the Committee's work programme. Conclude that a bank's ability to rely on ALA options in KSA depends on the jurisdiction's continuing eligibility under that Basel-supervised process, and that SAMA-level rules governing usage sit beneath this international framework; verify the current eligibility status rather than assuming the options remain permanently available.

clause_a.excerpt: Guidance on standards governing banks' usage of the options for alternative liquidity approaches (ALA) under LCR

clause_b.excerpt: The Basel Committee will oversee the independent peer review process for determining the eligibility of its member jurisdictions to adopt alternative treatment.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala_options||.why: When assessing whether a bank can rely on a committed liquidity facility to plug an HQLA shortfall, treat Option 1 as one of the ALA options that is only available subject to the general usage rules in Annex 3 — meaning it cannot exceed the actual currency shortfall and usage must be reported to the supervisor. The ALA guidance expressly flags that Option 1 typically requires central bank approval of the committed facility, so the facility is not self-executing. You should conclude that eligibility to count an Option 1 facility in the LCR depends both on SAMA/central bank approval and on the jurisdiction's demonstrated economic capacity to support it, not on the bank's election alone.

clause_a.locator: Page 69, Annex 3 / General rules (i) and para 3
clause_a.excerpt: For example, use of Option 1 will typically require central bank approval of the committed facility.

clause_b.excerpt: For Option 1 ... the jurisdiction must have the economic strength to support the committed liquidity facilities granted by its central bank.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala_options||.why: When evaluating whether a bank may hold foreign-currency HQLA to cover a domestic-currency liquidity need, read Option 2 as governed by the same ALA general rules (usage limited to the actual shortfall, supervisory reporting) plus its own currency-mismatch controls. The framework only permits Option 2 where the shortfall is genuine and the currency mismatch is 'justifiable and controlled within limits agreed by their supervisors,' with a haircut for FX risk. You should conclude that reliance on Option 2 is contingent on supervisor-agreed mismatch limits and freely/reliably convertible currencies — it is not a free substitution of any foreign HQLA.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank should not use an alternative treatment to meet its LCR more than its actual need as reflected by the shortfall of eligible HQLA.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_ala_options||.why: When considering whether a bank may hold Level 2A assets beyond the standard 40% cap, treat Option 3 as an ALA option subject to the general usage limits and to a stricter asset-quality gate: only Level 2A assets 'of a quality comparable to that for Level 1 assets' may exceed the cap, and they carry a minimum 20% haircut versus the ordinary 15%. Level 2B assets remain capped at 15% regardless. You should conclude that Option 3 does not relax quality standards — it tightens them (e.g. higher minimum ratings, higher haircut) — so counting excess Level 2A in the LCR depends on meeting those enhanced criteria, not merely on availability of Level 2A paper.

clause_a.excerpt: These additional Level 2A assets would be subject to a minimum haircut of 20%, ie 5% higher than the 15% haircut applicable to Level 2A assets that are included in the 40% cap.

clause_b.excerpt: the jurisdiction must only allow Level 2 assets that are of a quality ... comparable to that for Level 1 assets in its currency to be used under this option.

markdown_sama_en_3623_ver1_basel_committ.why: When assessing the durability of SAMA's authority to permit ALA treatment, note that eligibility is not self-certified: the independent peer review is conducted as part of the Basel Committee's work programme, and the Committee oversees the process determining a jurisdiction's eligibility to adopt alternative treatment. The jurisdiction must permit the review and 'address the comments made,' and may be required to re-assess ahead of schedule if circumstances change. You should conclude that the continued availability of ALA options underpinning any bank's LCR reliance is contingent on SAMA maintaining its peer-review standing — a condition external to the bank and subject to Basel Committee oversight.

clause_a.excerpt: The Basel Committee will oversee the independent peer review process for determining the eligibility of its member jurisdictions to adopt alternative treatment.

clause_b.excerpt: The jurisdiction must permit an independent peer review of its framework for alternative treatment to be conducted as part of the Basel Committee's work programme and address the comments made.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_aggregation_i.why: When scoping the obligations of an entity licensed for aggregation activity, do not read the Aggregation Instructions in isolation: clause 2.4 expressly provides they 'shall not prejudice' other SAMA instruments, and lists the Business Continuity Management Framework among the binding overlay. This means BCM requirements continue to apply to the aggregation entity independently of the Instructions' own technical/operational provisions. You should check the BCM Framework directly when assessing operational-resilience compliance, rather than assuming the Aggregation Instructions capture the full continuity obligation.

clause_a.excerpt: These Instructions shall not prejudice the provisions contained in relevant laws and instructions, including ... The Business Continuity Management Framework issued by SAMA.

clause_b.excerpt: The Business Continuity Management Framework issued by SAMA.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_aggregation_i.why: When assessing an aggregation entity's cybersecurity obligations, do not treat them as self-contained within these Instructions; the Instructions impose a standing duty to strengthen platform cybersecurity and immediately notify SAMA of any breach, which operates alongside SAMA's broader cyber and data-protection instructions referenced by the document. Article 2.4 states the Instructions 'shall not prejudice the provisions contained in relevant laws and instructions,' so any applicable SAMA cybersecurity framework continues to bind the entity in parallel. Conclude that breach-handling and notification duties must be read against SAMA's wider cyber regime rather than the aggregation text alone, and verify which specific SAMA framework applies to the licensed entity.

Article 1.2.6 defines Entity as 'an entity licensed by SAMA to practice aggregation activity,' and Article 2.2 confirms the Instructions apply to such licensed entities, so the duties in Sections II–III (accuracy verification, retention, cybersecurity, disclosure, contracting) all attach to this single defined role. Conclude that any obligation phrased 'the entity shall' is enforceable against the license holder, and that carrying out the activity without the SAMA license (Art 2.3) is itself prohibited.

clause_b.excerpt: Entity: An entity licensed by SAMA to practice aggregation activity.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_consumer||mar.why: When mapping consumer-protection duties, treat the Consumer as the protected beneficiary of the Entity's obligations rather than a party with symmetrical duties. Article 1.2.5 defines Consumer as 'a person to whom services are offered by the entity,' and Section II obligations (e.g. 8.5–8.7, 8.13, 8.14) require the entity to inform, educate, and deal fairly with that consumer, plus retain consumer files for at least 10 years and sign a contract clarifying rights and obligations. Conclude that consumer-facing failures — misleading information, non-disclosure of rejection reasons, inadequate contract terms — are enforceable breaches by the entity; note this 'Consumer' definition is finance-support specific and should not be conflated with the AML 'Customer' concept.

clause_a.excerpt: Consumer: A person to whom services are offered by the entity.

clause_b.excerpt: The entity shall consider the needs and desires of consumers and provide them with information in a clear, transparent and not misleading manner.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_entity||markd.why: When defining the aggregation entity's permissible dealings with lenders, recognise that the Entity–Financier relationship is tightly scoped and contractually mandated, not open commercial discretion. Article 1.2.4 defines Financier as banks, finance companies, and licensed finance entities, and the Instructions restrict the electronic linkage to aggregation purposes only (8.2), bar receiving/delivering funds on the financier's behalf without SAMA approval (8.8), prohibit favouring or marketing any financier (8.10), and require a written contract stating the financier's licensing number and service levels (Art 10). Conclude that the entity must remain a neutral conduit; check that any financier it lists is itself licensed and that the inter-party contract meets the Article 10 minimum content before relying on the arrangement.

clause_a.excerpt: The entity shall ensure that the electronic linkage between the entity and the financier serves the provision of aggregation activity only and is not used for any other purposes, unless approved by SAMA.

clause_b.excerpt: Financier: Banks, finance companies, and entities licensed to engage in finance activities under the laws applicable in Saudi Arabia.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_entity||markd.why: When scoping where the entity's data-security, confidentiality, and disclosure duties bite, note the Platform is the defined electronic channel through which the regulated activity and all consumer data flow. Article 1.2.7 defines Platform as 'any electronic means used to carry out the activity, including websites and applications,' and the entity must maintain/operate it (Art 3), safeguard confidentiality, security, integrity and availability of platform data (5.1–5.2), retain records for 10 years (5.3), and post terms and cybersecurity instructions on it (7.1, 8.1, 8.4). Conclude that platform-level failures — data disclosure without SAMA approval, missing pop-up acknowledgments, inadequate complaint feature — are directly attributable to the entity as breaches of these Instructions.

clause_a.excerpt: Ensure the security, integrity and availability of the information provided through the platform, including... the consumer’s personal information from loss and unauthorized access.

clause_b.excerpt: Platform: Any electronic means used to carry out the activity, including websites and applications.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_entity||markd.why: When determining who is legally bound by the Aggregation Activity Instructions and to whom they answer, read the 'Entity' as the sole licensed obligor and SAMA as the issuing/supervising authority whose approval gates key acts. The Instructions define 'Entity' as a body licensed by SAMA and 'SAMA' as the Saudi Central Bank issuing under the Finance Companies Control Law (Royal Decree M/51); numerous obligations (breach notification, funds handling, data disclosure) are triggered only 'unless SAMA's approval is obtained' or require immediate notification to SAMA. You should conclude that the entity cannot self-authorise the carve-out activities and must treat SAMA approval/notification as a precondition, not a formality.

clause_a.excerpt: In case of a breach, the entity shall immediately notify SAMA... The entity shall not receive or deliver funds on behalf of the financier unless SAMA's approval is obtained.

clause_b.excerpt: SAMA: The Saudi Central Bank... Entity: An entity licensed by SAMA to practice aggregation activity.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_cyber_securit.why: If you are scoping an aggregation entity's cybersecurity obligations, the CSF referenced at clause 2.4.3 of the Aggregation Instructions appears to be the same SAMA Cyber Security Framework document (SAMA_EN_3837), meaning the entity's platform-security and breach-notification duties should be read against that framework's control set and maturity model rather than as free-standing requirements. The Instructions state they 'shall not prejudice' the CSF and separately require the entity to strengthen platform cybersecurity, so the two operate cumulatively. Because this link is inferred from a name match rather than an explicit citation, verify in the primary CSF text that its stated scope ('Member Organizations') captures aggregation-activity licensees before relying on it as the governing standard.

clause_b.excerpt: The cyber security policy should include... a definition of general and specific responsibilities for cyber security.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_bcm_framework.why: When mapping the resilience obligations of an aggregation entity, the BCM Framework named at clause 2.4.4 of the Aggregation Instructions appears to be the SAMA Business Continuity Management Framework (SAMA_EN_3709), so the entity's continuity duties should be read against that framework's requirements. The Instructions provide they 'shall not prejudice' the BCM Framework, making the two cumulative rather than alternative. Because the link is inferred and the BCM Framework's stated audience is 'Member Organizations' (banks and their subsidiaries), verify in the primary text whether a finance-support/aggregation licensee falls within that defined scope before treating the framework's controls as binding on it.

clause_a.excerpt: These Instructions shall not prejudice the provisions... The Business Continuity Management Framework issued by SAMA.

clause_b.excerpt: All Member Organizations are required to comply with these requirements and integrate it formally in their BCM program.

markdown_sama_en_3689_ver1_bcm_framework.caveat: Inferred title match; the BCM Framework's 'Member Organization' scope (banks and banking subsidiaries) may not expressly cover aggregation licensees — confirm applicability before relying.

markdown_sama_en_3709_ver1_bcm_framework.why: When assessing whether a Member Organization's BCM program is compliant, treat BCM Governance as a mandatory constituent requirement of the Framework, not an optional best practice. The Framework (Section 2, Business Continuity Requirements) opens with clause 2.1 BCM Governance, which fixes board-level accountability, a mandated BCM committee, and a staffed BCM function. You should therefore check that ultimate responsibility sits with the board or a delegated executive and that the committee/charter/function exist, since absence of this governance layer is itself a Framework gap.

clause_a.excerpt: 2 Business Continuity Requirements 2.1 BCM Governance... The business continuity governance framework should be defined, approved, implemented and maintained.

clause_b.excerpt: Board of directors or a delegated executive member should have the ultimate responsibility for the BCM program.

markdown_sama_en_3709_ver1_bcm_framework.why: When evaluating BCM Framework compliance, treat BCM Strategy (clause 2.2) as a required Framework element that must be defined, approved, implemented and maintained, and aligned to the organization's strategic objectives. The Framework sets out the strategy's minimum content — long-term objectives, a road map with timelines, and requirements for continual review of alignment — so a program lacking a documented, approved strategy is non-compliant. You should confirm the strategy exists as an approved artefact and that its stated objectives and roadmap tie into the wider BCM program rather than sitting as an abstract statement.

clause_a.excerpt: The business continuity strategy should be defined, approved, implemented and maintained. The strategy should at minimum define: Long-term strategic objectives... Road map with timelines.

clause_b.excerpt: To ensure that business continuity Initiatives are in alignment with the strategic business objectives and embeds BCM as part of the good management practice.

markdown_sama_en_3709_ver1_bcm_framework.why: When scoping continuity obligations under SAMA circular 3709, treat the Business Continuity Plan (BCP) as a mandatory component the framework requires each Member Organization to define, approve, implement and maintain — not an optional deliverable. The framework's control considerations set the BCP as the operational plan enabling continued delivery of 'important and urgent activities' at a pre-defined level during disruption, and the framework mandates annual BCP simulation testing. A compliance reviewer should confirm the BCP exists, is board/committee-approved, and is exercised at least yearly, because its absence is a direct breach of the mandatory framework, not a best-practice gap.

clause_a.excerpt: All Member Organizations are required to comply with these requirements and integrate it formally in their BCM program.

clause_b.excerpt: A BCP should be defined, approved, implemented and maintained in readiness for use during disruptive incidents, to enable the Member organization to continue delivering its important and urgent activities

markdown_sama_en_3709_ver1_bcm_framework.why: When assessing whether a Member Organization's continuity program is defensible, check that the BIA and Risk Assessment were performed first, because the framework makes them the foundational inputs that drive RTOs, RPOs, MAO and the prioritized list of critical activities feeding the BCP and DRP. Section 2.4 mandates BIA/RA for all relevant activities and requires the BCM committee to endorse the prioritized list and defined recovery objectives. A reviewer should conclude that a BCP or DRP built without documented, committee-endorsed BIA/RA results is unsupported under the framework and its recovery targets cannot be relied upon.

clause_a.excerpt: The Member Organization should perform a business impact analysis and risk assessment for all relevant activities to determine the business continuity

clause_b.excerpt: The BCM committee should endorse the prioritized list, BIA results, RA and the defined RTOs, RPOs and MAOs.

markdown_sama_en_3709_ver1_bcm_framework.why: When mapping the framework's required documents, treat the Crisis Management Plan as a distinct mandatory component (section 2.8) separate from the BCP — it governs the response to major/declared incidents, including crisis declaration criteria and a command center, rather than routine activity recovery. The framework requires it to be defined, approved, implemented, monitored for compliance, and periodically evaluated, and BCP testing scenarios must cover activation of the crisis management team.
