Conclude that IRRBB1's numbers cannot be assessed in isolation from IRRBBA's stated assumptions, and that both are scoped to banks within the Basel supervisory-review IRRBB perimeter as adopted by that SAMA circular.

clause_a.excerpt: Template IRRBB1 provides quantitative IRRBB information, including the impact of interest rate shocks on their change in economic value of equity and net interest income.

clause_b.excerpt: Where significant modelling assumptions used in the bank's internal measurement systems (IMS)... are different from the modelling assumptions prescribed for the disclosure in Template IRRBB1, the...

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ccr||markdown.why: When determining which SAMA capital rules bind a bank's derivatives and SFT book, treat 'Counterparty Credit Risk' as a defined concept whose obligations live inside this framework document — the framework both defines CCR (Chapter 3) and sets the mandatory measurement, reporting and effective-date requirements around it. The framework fixes the go-live (01 January 2023) and the Q17 quarterly reporting duty within 30 days of quarter-end, so the concept is not free-standing guidance but an enforceable regime. Conclude that any CCR compliance position must be anchored to this document's provisions rather than to the abstract term.

clause_a.excerpt: Counterparty credit risk is defined in Chapter 3 of this framework. It is the risk that the counterparty to a transaction could default before the final settlement

clause_b.excerpt: This framework will be effective on 01 January 2023... report the Counterparty credit risk (CCR) and Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA)... within 30 days

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ccr_framework.why: When scoping capital obligations under this document, do not treat CCR and CVA as one undifferentiated charge — the framework carries a separate, mandatory CVA regime (Chapter 11) with its own covered-transaction scope and its own approach hierarchy. All banks with covered derivatives/SFTs must calculate a CVA risk capital requirement, and BA-CVA is the default unless SAMA approves SA-CVA; a materiality carve-out exists only below the SAR 446 billion notional threshold. Conclude that CVA capital is an independent standalone requirement (calculated on a 'CVA portfolio') that must be assessed on its own terms even after CCR EAD is measured.

clause_a.excerpt: The capital requirement for CVA risk must be calculated by all banks involved in covered transactions in both banking book and trading book.

clause_b.excerpt: Two approaches are available for calculating CVA capital... Banks must use the BA-CVA unless they receive approval from Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) to use the SA-CVA.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ccr_framework.why: When advising on whether a bank may use its own internal exposure models for CCR, note that IMM is a permission-gated method inside this framework, not a default option — a bank must obtain SAMA approval, meet the qualifying standards (7.6–7.60), and generally apply IMM to all exposures subject to CCR except long settlement transactions. Reversion to the standardized approach is only allowed under exceptional circumstances or for immaterial exposures and must not enable regulatory-capital arbitrage. Conclude that IMM use should be verified against an actual SAMA approval and the use-test/track-record conditions before relying on internally-modelled EAD.

clause_a.excerpt: Banks that use the BA-CVA or the SA-CVA for calculating CVA capital requirements may cap the maturity adjustment factor at 1... when they calculate CCR capital requirements under the Internal Ratings Based (IRB) app[roach]

clause_b.excerpt: A bank that wishes to adopt an internal models method to measure exposure or exposure at default (EAD) for regulatory capital purposes must seek SAMA approval.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ccr_framework.why: When determining the default CCR measurement method, treat SA-CCR as the mandatory fallback: this framework requires banks without IMM approval to use SA-CCR for OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and long settlement transactions. The framework also links the CVA regime to SA-CCR outputs — the IRB maturity-adjustment cap at 1 applies per netting set for which BA-CVA/SA-CVA capital is calculated. Conclude that unless a bank holds IMM approval, SA-CCR governs its derivative EAD, and CVA-related maturity caps must be applied consistently across the CCR and CVA calculations.

clause_a.excerpt: Banks that use the BA-CVA or the SA-CVA for calculating CVA capital requirements may cap the maturity adjustment factor at 1 for all netting sets

clause_b.excerpt: The Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) applies to over the-counter (OTC) derivatives... Banks that do not have approval to apply the internal model method (IMM)... must use SA-CCR

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ccp_exposures.why: When calculating exposures to central counterparties, do not assume the ordinary bilateral SA-CCR netting rules apply unchanged — Chapter 8 recognises that CCP netting arrangements are less standardized and makes specific adjustments. Net replacement cost for CCP trade exposures may be used only where close-out netting meets the requirements cross-referenced in 8.10, which expressly incorporate SA-CCR provisions 6.9–6.10 for derivative transactions. Conclude that CCP exposure treatment borrows SA-CCR's netting-eligibility tests as a precondition, so those SA-CCR clauses must be satisfied before netting benefit is claimed against CCP exposures.

clause_a.excerpt: the total replacement cost of all contracts relevant to the trade exposure determination can be calculated as a net replacement cost if the applicable close-out netting sets meet the requirements set out in: ...6.9 and 6.10 of the SA-CCR

clause_b.excerpt: The Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) applies to over the-counter (OTC) derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and long settlement transactions.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_default_fund|.why: When scoping capital requirements for a clearing member bank's CCP exposures, treat default fund contributions as a distinct workstream governed by Chapter 8, not the SA-CCR chapter — the two are linked but sequential. SA-CCR (Chapter 6) computes counterparty credit risk EAD for OTC derivatives and long settlement transactions, while default fund contributions to a QCCP are capitalized via the separate risk-sensitive KCMi formula in Chapter 8 which itself draws on the hypothetical capital requirement KCCP. The practical consequence: verify you have applied Chapter 8's formulae (and the QCCP cap in 8.40) to fund contributions rather than defaulting to SA-CCR, and confirm you have the CCP-supplied inputs (KCCP, prefunded contributions) required under 8.37.

clause_a.excerpt: Clearing member banks will apply a risk weight to their default fund contributions determined according to a risk sensitive formula

clause_b.excerpt: The Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) applies to over the-counter (OTC) derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and long settlement transactions.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_addon_ir||mar.why: When computing potential future exposure under SA-CCR, the interest rate derivative add-on is a component within that method, not a standalone regime — so its maturity-bucket allocation and aggregation rules only bite once you are inside SA-CCR (i.e. no IMM approval for the relevant trades). The add-on for interest rate derivatives (6.59) feeds the netting-set aggregate add-on described in SA-CCR's PFE section, and note that supervisory correlation parameters do not apply to interest rate derivatives — a scope carve-out you must respect. Practical consequence: apply the IR add-on only within the SA-CCR EAD calculation and confirm you are using the correct maturity-bucket offsetting rather than importing the equity/credit/commodity correlation treatment.

clause_a.excerpt: The calculation of the add-on for the interest rate derivative asset class captures the risk of interest rate derivatives of different maturities being imperfectly correlated.

clause_b.excerpt: Banks that do not have approval to apply the internal model method (IMM) for the relevant transactions must use SA-CCR, as set out in this chapter.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ead||markdown.why: When determining counterparty credit risk RWA, understand that EAD is the output SA-CCR produces and the input the credit-risk approaches consume — they are chained, not interchangeable. SA-CCR calculates EAD per netting set (EAD = alpha × (RC + PFE)), and that EAD is then risk-weighted under the standardized or IRB approach (5.12), unless the bank has SAMA approval for IMM as an alternative EAD method. Practical consequence: confirm which EAD method applies (SA-CCR by default, IMM only with SAMA approval) before applying risk weights, and check the exemptions in 5.15 where EAD is zero for certain hedged/guarantee transactions.

clause_a.excerpt: the exposure amount or EAD for a given counterparty is equal to the sum of the exposure amounts

clause_b.excerpt: EAD is to be calculated separately for each netting set

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_qccp||markdow.why: When capitalizing CCP-cleared derivatives, whether a counterparty is a QCCP determines the capital track — but SA-CCR still supplies the underlying EAD before preferential QCCP treatment applies. QCCP status triggers the favorable 2% trade-exposure risk weight and Chapter 8 default-fund treatment, while a non-qualifying CCP attracts the standardized approach for trade exposure and a 1250% weight on fund contributions (8.41-8.42); the QCCP definition (4.2) also conditions on the CCP meeting 8.37's data-sharing requirements. Practical consequence: verify QCCP status (including SAMA's determination where no compliant CCP regulator exists) and note the three-month grace window when a CCP loses QCCP status, then confirm SA-CCR EAD is computed as the basis before applying the QCCP risk weights.

clause_a.excerpt: Regardless of whether a central counterparty (CCP) is classified as a qualifying CCP (QCCP), a bank retains the responsibility to ensure that it maintains adequate capital for its exposures.

clause_b.excerpt: The Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) applies to over the-counter (OTC) derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and long settlement transactions.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_replacement_c.why: When calculating SA-CCR EAD, replacement cost is one of its two defining inputs (EAD = alpha × (RC + PFE)) and must be computed differently for margined versus unmargined netting sets. For margined trades RC uses the formula RC = max{V − C; TH + MTA − NICA; 0} (6.20), where the third zero term prevents a negative RC and margin agreement terms (threshold, MTA, NICA) directly reduce or increase the figure. Practical consequence: confirm you have correctly classified each netting set as margined or unmargined — a one-way agreement where only the bank posts VM is treated as unmargined — and that collateral and independent amounts are fed into the correct RC term rather than double-counted.

clause_a.excerpt: they relate to the formulation of replacement cost for margined trades, as set out in 6.20: RC = max{V − C; RH + MTA − MHXA; 0}

clause_b.excerpt: The replacement cost (RC) and the potential future exposure (PFE) components are calculated differently for margined and unmargined netting sets.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_saccr||markdo.why: When assessing whether a bank has correctly computed EAD under SA-CCR, treat the sample portfolio section as the authoritative worked illustration of the same rules, not as a separate standard. Both sit within the one CCR framework: the SA-CCR chapter (6.1) sets the binding methodology for OTC, exchange-traded and long settlement transactions, and Section 12 explicitly applies that method to five sample portfolios using the EAD formula with alpha=1.4. For a compliance review you would use the examples to test the bank's calculation logic against SAMA's intended application, but the enforceable obligation remains the SA-CCR chapter itself.

clause_a.excerpt: The Standardized Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR) applies to over the-counter (OTC) derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives and long settlement transactions.

clause_b.excerpt: This section sets out the calculation of exposure at default (EAD) for five sample portfolios using SA-CCR.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_alpha||markdo.why: When reviewing a bank's IMM EAD figure, check the alpha parameter as a distinct supervisory lever, because IMM does not merely output an exposure — it multiplies Effective EPE by alpha to produce regulatory EAD. Alpha is fixed at 1.4 by default, but SAMA may impose a higher value for concentrated or wrong-way-risk exposures, and internal alpha estimates require SAMA approval and are floored at 1.2. You would therefore confirm which alpha applies and whether any own-estimate was formally approved before relying on the bank's IMM capital number.

clause_a.excerpt: Alpha (α) is set equal to 1.4. SAMA may require a higher alpha... Banks should seek approval from SAMA to compute internal estimates of alpha subject to a floor of 1.2

clause_b.excerpt: A bank that wishes to adopt an internal models method to measure exposure or exposure at default (EAD) for regulatory capital purposes must seek SAMA approval.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_backtesting||.why: When judging whether a bank's IMM approval is defensible, treat backtesting and ongoing model validation as an integral, mandatory condition of IMM eligibility rather than good practice. The IMM chapter conditions approval on meeting requirements 7.6–7.60, and those provisions require pre-approval backtesting over multiple horizons, ongoing validation, and permit SAMA to demand corrective action or additional capital where realized exposures diverge from forecasts. You would therefore verify the validation record exists and is current, since deficient backtesting can justify SAMA imposing higher capital or withdrawing IMM reliance.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank must carry out backtesting using historical data... Significant differences between realized exposures and the forecast distribution... SAMA may require additional capital

clause_b.excerpt: The bank must satisfy SAMA that, in addition to meeting the operational requirements identified in 7.36 to 7.60 below, it adheres to sound practices for CCR management

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_cross_product.why: When assessing whether a bank may net across SFTs and OTC derivatives for capital purposes, note that cross-product netting is available only within IMM, not as a general entitlement. The rules state expressly that the Cross-Product Netting Rules (7.61–7.71) apply to netting across SFTs, or across SFTs and OTC derivatives, for regulatory capital computation under IMM, and require a written bilateral arrangement plus reasoned legal opinions of enforceability across all relevant jurisdictions. You would therefore confirm the bank holds IMM approval and the requisite legal opinions before accepting any cross-product netting benefit in its capital figures.

clause_a.excerpt: The Cross-Product Netting Rules apply specifically to netting across SFTs, or to netting across both SFTs and OTC derivatives, for purposes of regulatory capital computation under IMM.

clause_b.excerpt: A bank may also choose to adopt an internal models method to measure counterparty credit risk (CCR)... to only OTC derivatives, to only SFTs, or to both, subject to the appropriate recognition of netting specified in 7.61 to 7.71.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_imm||markdown.why: When checking IMM exposure figures, confirm the unit of measurement is the netting set as defined in the framework, because IMM measures CCR exposure or EAD at netting-set level, not per trade. Paragraph 7.6 states EAD is measured at the netting set defined in Chapter 4 and 7.61–7.71, so an incorrectly constituted netting set (or improper aggregation of collateral and margin agreements) directly distorts the capital outcome. You would therefore verify that trades are validly grouped into legally enforceable netting sets before relying on the aggregated IMM EAD.

clause_a.excerpt: CCR exposure or EAD is measured at the level of the netting set as defined in Chapter 4 of this framework and 7.61 to 7.71 of this framework.

clause_b.excerpt: Where a single margin agreement applies to several netting sets... collateral will be exchanged based on mark-to-market values that are netted across all transactions

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_imm||markdown.why: When assessing whether your bank can use internal models to measure CCR exposure/EAD for capital purposes, treat this as a supervisory gating requirement, not a self-selected option: the IMM cannot be used without prior SAMA approval, and SAMA also sets the conditions for reversion and continued eligibility. This link is grounded in the requirement that a bank 'must seek SAMA approval' and 'must satisfy SAMA' on sound CCR practices before applying models for capital adequacy. Conclude that IMM eligibility, scope, phase-in plans and any reversion to the standardized approach are all conditional on SAMA's determination, so you cannot rely on internal model outputs for regulatory capital until that approval is documented.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank that wishes to adopt an internal models method to measure exposure or exposure at default (EAD) for regulatory capital purposes must seek SAMA approval.

clause_b.excerpt: Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) Minimum Capital Requirements for Counterparty Credit Risk (CCR) and Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA)

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_imm||markdown.why: If your bank uses or seeks to use the IMM, do not treat stress testing as a separable exercise: it is an embedded qualifying condition of IMM approval, so failure to run the prescribed CCR stress program undermines the model's regulatory acceptability. The framework places the stress-testing mandate (7.46) inside the IMM operational requirements (7.36–7.60) that a bank 'must meet all' to adopt the method, requiring monthly single-factor and at-least-quarterly multifactor and joint exposure/creditworthiness stress testing with senior-management ownership. Conclude that an IMM firm must be able to evidence the full stress-testing elements set out here; gaps in that program are a direct IMM compliance deficiency, not merely a risk-management shortfall.

clause_a.excerpt: The bank must meet all of the requirements given in 7.6 to 7.60 and must apply the method to all of its exposures that are subject to counterparty credit risk.

clause_b.excerpt: Banks must have a comprehensive stress testing program for counterparty credit risk. The stress testing program must include the following elements.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_imm||markdown.why: When evaluating IMM eligibility, treat wrong-way risk identification and monitoring as a mandatory qualifying element rather than optional analytics: it sits within the 7.36–7.60 operational requirements the bank 'must meet all' of to adopt the method. Provision 7.47 obliges banks to identify general wrong-way risk exposures, design stress/scenario testing around risk factors positively correlated with counterparty creditworthiness, monitor by product/region/industry, and report to senior management and the Board. Conclude that an IMM firm must demonstrate specific wrong-way risk (7.48) and general wrong-way risk governance to SAMA; absence of this analysis is a defect in the model's qualifying standards.

clause_a.excerpt: in addition to meeting the operational requirements identified in 7.36 to 7.60 below, it adheres to sound practices for CCR management.

clause_b.excerpt: Banks must identify exposures that give rise to a greater degree of general wrong-way risk. Stress testing and scenario analyses must be designed to identify risk factors that are positively correlated with counterparty credit worthiness.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_imm||markdown.why: When mapping capital obligations, keep CCR/IMM exposure measurement distinct from the CVA capital requirement: they are separate charges applying to the same covered transactions, and the CVA framework uses 'regulatory CVA' (excluding the bank's own default) computed per counterparty. Chapter 11 requires the CVA capital requirement to be calculated by all banks in covered transactions in both banking and trading books, independent of the exposure method used for CCR. Conclude that IMM approval for CCR does not discharge CVA obligations; you must separately calculate regulatory CVA (via BA-CVA by default, or SA-CVA with SAMA approval) for each counterparty with a covered position.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank that wishes to adopt an internal models method to measure exposure or exposure at default (EAD) for regulatory capital purposes must seek SAMA approval.

clause_b.excerpt: A bank must calculate regulatory CVA for each counterparty with which it has at least one covered position for the purpose of the CVA risk capital requirements.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ba_cva||markd.why: When determining which CVA capital method applies, start from the default rule: BA-CVA is the mandatory approach under the CVA framework unless SAMA has granted approval to use SA-CVA. Chapter 11 (11.7) establishes the two available approaches and expressly makes BA-CVA the fallback, so the BA-CVA node is a subordinate method within the overarching CVA framework. Conclude that a bank may only rely on SA-CVA where it holds documented SAMA approval; otherwise it must apply BA-CVA (or, below the 446 billion SAR non-centrally-cleared notional threshold, the permitted alternative treatment).

clause_a.excerpt: Banks must use the BA-CVA unless they receive approval from Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) to use the SA-CVA.

clause_b.excerpt: 11. Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework ... The risk-weighted assets for Credit Value Adjustment risk are determined by multiplying the capital requirements...

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_cva_framework.why: When determining which CVA capital methodology a bank may lawfully use, treat SA-CVA as a permission-gated option under the overarching CVA Framework, not a free choice. Chapter 11 of the Framework establishes the CVA regime and expressly makes BA-CVA the default, allowing SA-CVA only where SAMA has approved its use. A compliance reviewer should therefore verify that any SA-CVA reliance is backed by an actual SAMA approval and note that approval may be partial (limited to certain transactions within a netting set).

clause_a.excerpt: Two approaches are available for calculating CVA capital: the standardized approach (SA-CVA) and the basic approach (BA-CVA).

clause_b.excerpt: Banks must use the BA-CVA unless they receive approval from Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) to use the SA-CVA.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ba_cva||markd.why: When assessing a bank's BA-CVA capital number, check whether it recognizes hedges, because hedge recognition is only permitted for hedges meeting the Framework's eligibility criteria and only under the full version of BA-CVA. Art 11.10 ties eligibility of CVA hedges specifically to paragraphs 11.17–11.19 for BA-CVA, and the reduced version eliminates hedging recognition entirely. A reviewer should conclude that a bank claiming hedge offsets under BA-CVA must be using the full version and must demonstrate each hedge meets the stated eligibility conditions; unrecognized or ineligible hedges cannot reduce the BA-CVA charge.

clause_a.excerpt: The reduced version eliminates the element of hedging recognition from the full version.

clause_b.excerpt: Eligibility criteria for CVA hedges are specified in 11.17 to 11.19 for the BA-CVA and in 11.37 to 11.39 for the SA-CVA.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ba_cva||markd.why: The linked node here is the SA-CVA supervisory risk-weight/sensitivity machinery (delta and vega sensitivities), which belongs to the SA-CVA calculation, not BA-CVA. For a compliance reviewer, the practical point is that the two approaches use different inputs: BA-CVA works from counterparty-level supervisory weights and hedge recognition, while the sensitivity-based supervisory risk weights (11.46–11.53) apply to banks approved for SA-CVA. Confirm which approach a bank is actually approved for before deciding which risk-weight provisions govern its capital number.

clause_a.excerpt: the standardized approach (SA-CVA) and the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks must use the BA-CVA unless they receive approval...

clause_b.excerpt: A bank may use AAD and similar computational techniques to calculate CVA sensitivities under the SA-CVA if doing so is consistent...

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ba_cva||markd.caveat: The 'CVA Supervisory Risk Weights' node content shown (11.46-11.53 sensitivities) is SA-CVA machinery; the link to BA-CVA is via the shared Chapter 11 regime rather than a direct BA-CVA computation. Verify the primary text before treating these risk weights as applicable to a BA-CVA bank.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ba_cva||markd.why: When reviewing a BA-CVA capital figure, understand that Stand-alone CVA capital (SCVAc) is the per-counterparty building block from which the BA-CVA total is aggregated. The reduced version of BA-CVA computes the charge by summing each counterparty's SCVAc contribution and applying the 0.65 discount scalar, so SCVAc is definitionally part of the BA-CVA calculation. A reviewer checking a BA-CVA number should trace it back to correctly determined counterparty-level SCVAc inputs before accepting the aggregate.

clause_a.excerpt: The capital requirement for CVA risk under the reduced version of the BA-CVA ... where the discount scalar ... = 0.65 ... summations are taken over all counterparties

clause_b.excerpt: SCVAc is the CVA capital requirement that counterparty c would [contribute]

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ba_cva||markd.caveat: Node B's defining formula text is partly OCR-garbled; the SCVAc definition is inferred from the reduced BA-CVA summation. Confirm the exact SCVAc formula in the primary text.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_cva_hedges||m.why: When assessing hedge offsets claimed by a bank on SA-CVA, note that eligibility of CVA hedges under SA-CVA is governed by a distinct set of criteria (11.37–11.39) from those applying to BA-CVA (11.17–11.19). Art 11.10 assigns separate eligibility rules per approach, so a hedge recognized under one approach is not automatically recognized under the other. A reviewer should confirm the bank applied the SA-CVA-specific eligibility conditions before treating hedges as reducing the SA-CVA capital charge.

clause_a.excerpt: Eligibility criteria for CVA hedges are specified in 11.17 to 11.19 for the BA-CVA and in 11.37 to 11.39 for the SA-CVA.

clause_b.excerpt: the standardized approach (SA-CVA) ... Banks must use the BA-CVA unless they receive approval ... to use the SA-CVA.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_regulatory_cv.why: When determining which CVA capital methodology a bank must apply, treat 'regulatory CVA' as the required input measure that feeds the SA-CVA, not as an interchangeable concept. The framework defines regulatory CVA (excluding the bank's own default, with best-practice accounting constraints) and then states the SA-CVA uses as inputs the sensitivities of that regulatory CVA to credit spreads and market risk factors; SA-CVA use is conditional on SAMA approval, otherwise BA-CVA applies. A reader should conclude that eligibility for SA-CVA depends on being able to compute regulatory CVA and its sensitivities per Chapter 11, and should not assume SA-CVA can be used without both SAMA approval and a compliant regulatory CVA calculation.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank must calculate regulatory CVA for each counterparty with which it has at least one covered position for the purpose of the CVA risk capital requirements.

clause_b.excerpt: The SA-CVA uses as inputs the sensitivities of regulatory CVA to counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors driving the values of covered transactions.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_sa_cva||markd.why: When scoping what a bank must be able to compute before it can use SA-CVA, note that the delta and vega sensitivities are the operative measurement inputs the approach depends on, not an optional add-on. The framework states the SA-CVA uses sensitivities of regulatory CVA as inputs, and eligibility requires the bank to calculate CVA and CVA sensitivities at least monthly; the sensitivity provisions (11.46-11.53) then specify that vega sensitivities are always material and must be calculated regardless of whether the portfolio contains options. A reader should conclude that a bank cannot qualify for or apply SA-CVA without producing both delta and vega sensitivities per these paragraphs, and vega cannot be omitted on the grounds of no options exposure.

clause_a.excerpt: A bank must be able to model exposure and calculate, on at least a monthly basis, CVA and CVA sensitivities to the market risk factors specified...

clause_b.excerpt: CVA sensitivities for vega risk are always material and must be calculated regardless of whether or not the portfolio includes options.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_sa_cva||markd.why: When deciding whether a bank may use SA-CVA rather than the default BA-CVA, treat SAMA as the gatekeeper: use of SA-CVA is not a bank election but requires prior SAMA approval, which may also be limited in scope. The framework provides that banks must use BA-CVA unless they receive SAMA approval for SA-CVA, and separately allows SAMA to determine materiality and to grant partial approvals covering only some transactions in a netting set. A reader should conclude that any reliance on SA-CVA must be backed by documented SAMA approval and should verify the exact scope of that approval before applying SA-CVA across a portfolio.

clause_a.excerpt: Banks must use the BA-CVA unless they receive approval from Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) to use the SA-CVA.

clause_b.excerpt: SAMA approval to use the SA-CVA is limited and does not cover all transactions within a legal netting set.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ead||markdown.why: When computing EAD under the SA-CCR, treat replacement cost as a defined component of the EAD formula, not a separate calculation: EAD equals alpha (1.4) times the sum of RC and PFE. The framework defines RC per paragraphs 6.5 to 6.21 and current exposure/RC as the loss that would occur on immediate counterparty default, and the EAD formula incorporates that RC directly. A reader should conclude that any EAD figure depends on a correctly derived RC (margined vs unmargined) and should trace the RC inputs before relying on the EAD output.

clause_a.excerpt: RC = the replacement cost calculated according to 6.5 to 6.21 ... EAD = alpha * (RC + PFE)

clause_b.excerpt: For unmargined transactions, the RC intends to capture the loss that would occur if a counterparty were to default and were closed out of its transactions immediately.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_margin_agreem.why: When calculating RC, first determine whether a margin agreement applies, because it changes the RC formula: margined netting sets use the max{V-C; TH+MTA-NICA; 0} formulation while unmargined sets use a simpler close-out measure. The framework classifies a netting set as margined only where the counterparty must post variation margin (one-way agreements where only the bank posts are treated as unmargined), and NICA feeds directly into the margined RC formula illustrated in the worked examples. A reader should conclude that RC and thus EAD turn on the correct characterization of the margin agreement and the NICA computation, and should check whether the agreement obliges the counterparty to post VM before applying the margined formula.

clause_a.excerpt: Margined netting sets are netting sets covered by a margin agreement under which the bank's counterparty has to post variation margin; all other netting sets ... are treated as unmargined.

clause_b.excerpt: RC = max{V - C; TH + MTA - NICA; 0} ... relate to the formulation of replacement cost for margined trades.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_nica||markdow.why: When determining regulatory capital for margined derivatives under SA-CCR, you cannot treat NICA and Replacement Cost as separate inputs — NICA is an explicit term inside the RC formula. Under paragraph 6.20/6.21, RC = max{V − C; TH + MTA − NICA; 0}, so the net independent collateral posted by the counterparty (less unsegregated collateral the bank posted) directly reduces the exposure figure that feeds EAD. markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_ead||markdown.why: When determining a bank's total counterparty-credit-risk capital under this framework, treat EAD and the CVA charge as two distinct but connected outputs rather than one figure. EAD (Chapter 5–8) quantifies exposure to default, while the CVA capital requirement—of which SCVAc is the stand-alone per-counterparty component under the reduced BA-CVA—captures losses from changing CVA values driven by counterparty spread and market moves; both apply to the same covered derivative and SFT populations. For a compliance decision, conclude that a bank in scope must compute and hold capital for both, and that recognizing collateral or hedges in one calculation constrains what can be recognized in the other (e.g. LGD limits when collateral is in EAD).

For a compliance decision, verify the CCP's QCCP status and note the transitional rule: if a CCP ceases to qualify, trades may continue to be capitalized as QCCP exposures for three months unless SAMA requires otherwise—but adequate-capital responsibility under Pillar 2 persists regardless of QCCP status.

The consequence: if the adjusted notional is mis-specified (wrong currency leg, missing duration adjustment, or wrong treatment of variable/leveraged notionals under 6.39), every downstream effective notional and add-on is wrong, so a capital-charge review must first confirm the correct adjusted-notional definition was applied per asset class.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_effective_not.why: When calculating effective notional, note the maturity factor (MF) is one of its three mandatory multiplicative terms and its formula differs by whether the netting set is margined or unmargined. Per 6.51 the unmargined MF uses the lesser of one year and remaining maturity floored at ten business days, while 6.53 requires margined trades to use the margin period of risk subject to specified floors — so the same trade produces a different effective notional depending on collateral arrangements. The consequence: when reviewing a capital charge you must confirm the correct MF branch (margined vs unmargined) and the applicable floor were used, because choosing the wrong maturity-factor rule directly distorts effective notional and therefore the add-on.

markdown_sama_en_4283_ver1_margin_period.why: When computing the maturity factor for margined netting sets, the margin period of risk (MPOR) is the driving input and is subject to floors that can be raised in defined circumstances. The consequence: before relying on a margined maturity factor, check whether any of the 6.54 exceptions apply, because a triggered higher MPOR floor raises the maturity factor and thus the effective notional and capital charge — this is an enforceable adjustment, not optional.

Both derive from the same Chapter 11 framework, which sets the CVA portfolio on a standalone basis (para 11.6) and prescribes the sensitivity-based procedures (11.47-11.53). Conclude that a DTFC cannot treat 20% as a fixed ceiling — SAMA retains discretion to set a firm-specific higher minimum, and capital planning must reconcile total capital against reported shareholders' funds.

clause_a.excerpt: maintain records ... to enable proper computation of the institution's capital adequacy of 20%; and maintain the prescribed minimum capital requirements

clause_b.excerpt: SAMA may require higher minimum capital ratios for an individual DTFC based on, but not limited to the following criteria

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1||markdown_sam.why: When mapping a DTFC's governance and control obligations, note that the Corporate Governance and Risk Management chapter imposes mandatory, proportionate arrangements including per-senior-manager job descriptions tied to SAMA fit-and-proper pre-approval and a maintained Management Responsibilities Description Document (MRDD). Critically, this chapter's related provisions also carry the AML/CTF supervisory-officer and ongoing-monitoring duties — the Compliance Officer coordinates with Internal Audit, must have unrestricted access to customer and transaction records, and DTFCs must monitor, risk-classify and report suspicious activity to the Financial Investigation Unit and SAMA. Conclude that governance and AML functions here are intertwined obligations of the same firm and must be scoped together, and that senior-manager appointments require SAMA pre-approval.

clause_a.excerpt: DTFCs are also required to comply with the Finance Companies Control Law, SAMA regulations for Finance Companies (FCs), and other relevant laws and regulations

clause_b.excerpt: robust governance and risk management arrangements... Be included in every application to SAMA for pre-approval as a senior manager... report these to the Financial Investigation Unit, and inform SAMA

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1||markdown_sam.why: When determining whether these Regulations apply to a given firm, the defined term 'Deposit Taking Finance Company' is the scoping gate: the rules apply only to finance companies authorized to mobilize savings and time deposits from non-individual customers and to lend out of those deposits, subject to the Finance Companies Control Law (Royal Decree M/51). The definition also frames the account architecture — General Accounts exist solely to facilitate Term Deposit Accounts, with strict linking, name-matching and permitted-credit-source rules. Conclude that a firm not authorised for deposit-taking falls outside this instrument (though still bound by general FC rules), and that the DTFC's deposit operations must respect the closed funding channels and remitter name-matching controls defined for the General Account.

clause_a.excerpt: These SAMA regulations are applicable to all Deposit Taking Finance Companies (DTFCs) operating in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA)

clause_b.excerpt: finance companies that are authorized to mobilize savings and time deposits from non-individual customers... DTFC must match the name of remitter with the name on General Account

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1||markdown_sam.why: When assessing prudential exposure for a Deposit Taking Finance Company, treat the Liquidity Requirements chapter as an operative, quantified obligation embedded in the parent DTFC Regulations 2020, not a soft standard. Chapter 5 imposes hard, enforceable minimums — a 20% liquid-asset holding against deposit liabilities, a statutory deposit with SAMA of not less than 4%, a 15x cap of deposit liabilities to total capital, and monthly Appendix B liquidity returns due by the 15th business day. You should conclude these ratios are binding licence conditions for any DTFC authorized to mobilize deposits, and check both the reporting deadline mechanics and the remedial one-month window for breaching the 15x cap.

clause_a.excerpt: observing liquidity ratios with regard to its liquid assets vis-a-vis total deposit liabilities and other prudential regulations as prescribed for DTFCs

clause_b.excerpt: Every DTFC shall maintain a minimum holding of liquid assets of twenty per cent (20%) of all its deposit liabilities... a statutory deposits of a sum not less than 4%

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_account_openi.why: When advising a DTFC on onboarding, do not treat the account-opening documentation rules and the KYC standards as separable checklists — they operate as one gate to opening any account. Chapter 8 fixes the minimum identity data and beneficial-owner acknowledgement required (including that the account holder is the real beneficiary), while Chapter 13 makes clear identity establishment, customer-acceptance policy and purpose/BO verification are mandatory KYC preconditions; if KYC suspicions arise on accuracy or sufficiency, the DTFC must refuse to open, refuse the relationship, refuse transactions, and report to SAMA's FIU. You should conclude that satisfying the account-opening document list alone is insufficient — the opening decision must also clear the KYC acceptance and BO-verification standard, and remote opening for new customers remains prohibited.

clause_a.excerpt: Acknowledges and verify that Account holder is the real beneficiary of the account.

clause_b.excerpt: the DTFCs shall not allow to open the account, start the relationship or execute any transactions. DTFCs must information Financial Investigation Unit at SAMA about the suspicions.

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_fiu||markdown.why: When mapping a DTFC's AML reporting duties, read the KYC obligation as the trigger and the SAMA Financial Investigation Unit as the mandatory recipient. Chapter 13 requires that where KYC concerns (accuracy, correctness, insufficient data, or non-compliance) prevent opening, the DTFC must decline the relationship and inform the FIU at SAMA of the suspicions; ongoing monitoring likewise routes suspicious transactions to the FIU. You should conclude that suspicion identified through KYC/monitoring is not discretionary intelligence — it is an escalation obligation to a named SAMA body, and refusal to onboard does not discharge the separate duty to report.

clause_a.excerpt: DTFCs must information Financial Investigation Unit at SAMA about the suspicions.

clause_b.excerpt: customer acceptance policy, customer identification as set in these Rules (at minimum), on-going monitoring of high-risk accounts, and risk management

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_kyc||markdown.why: When determining the legal source of a DTFC's AML/CTF duties, note that the DTFC KYC chapter and the Law on Combating the Financing of Terrorism *appear* to operate in the same regime, but the KYC chapter here is SAMA sectoral rule-making while the CTF Law is primary legislation carrying its own reporting, supervisory-sanction and Financial Intelligence Directorate architecture. The KYC chapter itself directs suspicion reporting to SAMA's FIU and requires conformity with statutory requirements on terrorism-finance prevention, which links conceptually to the CTF Law's regime for suspicious transaction reporting and supervisory penalties (up to SAR 5,000,000 per violation). Treat this as a lead: verify the CTF Law and its Implementing Regulation (and the AML Law) directly to confirm which reporting channel, defined terms, and penalty exposure actually bind the DTFC, since the DTFC chapter does not itself cite the CTF Law.

clause_a.excerpt: policies and procedures at least conform with local statutory and regulatory requirements with respect to money laundering and terrorism finance prevention

clause_b.excerpt: Impose a monetary fine of up to 5.000.000 riyals per violation

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_corp_governan.why: When assessing a DTFC's senior-management appointments, treat the corporate-governance obligation and the Fit and Proper regime as a single gating process. Chapter 3 requires a Job Description for each senior manager that must be included in every application to SAMA for pre-approval 'as per SAMA's fit and proper regulations,' and re-submitted on any significant change of responsibilities. You should conclude that senior manager pre-approval is conditioned on the separate SAMA Fit and Proper Regulations — so a governance structure cannot be evidenced as complete without confirming each pre-approval and JD/MRDD was processed under that fit-and-proper standard.

clause_b.excerpt: be updated and resubmitted if there is a significant change to the senior manager's responsibilities as per SAMA's fit and proper regulations

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_closing_accou.why: When advising a Deposit-Taking Finance Company (DTFC) on the full lifecycle of a General Account, treat closing rules and opening/funding rules as a single continuous regime rather than isolated chapters. The opening rules fix the source-of-funds principle (General Account may only be credited from the accountholder's own bank account or linked Term Deposit Account), and the closing/withdrawal rules enforce the mirror: funds must be remitted back to the same bank account from which the General Account was initially funded. You should therefore conclude that at closing you cannot pay out to an unrelated third-party account, and that the audit trail captured at opening (remitter name, IBAN) governs where money may legitimately return.

clause_a.excerpt: Finance must remit the funds back to the same Bank account of the account holder from which General Account was initially funded i.e. the source.

clause_b.excerpt: General Account can ONLY be funded... DTFC must match the name of remitter with the name on General Account before crediting the funds.

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_dtfc_general_.why: When scoping a DTFC's ongoing obligations for General Accounts, do not read the opening rules as the end of the diligence duty — the freezing/updating chapter converts the account-opening acknowledgements into live enforcement triggers. The opening agreement obliges the customer to renew ID documents and consents to freezing if data is not updated, and Chapter 11 makes freezing mandatory (e.g. within 90 days of expiry of the juristic entity's authorization). You should conclude that the DTFC must monitor validity of IDs and authorizations continuously and freeze non-compliant accounts, and that the contractual freeze right documented at opening is what makes that action legally clean.

clause_a.excerpt: Acknowledges that the DTFC will freeze the account if account holder does not update or renew its data.

clause_b.excerpt: All DTFCs must freeze all General Accounts of juristic entities after 90 days from the expiration date of the respective authorization.

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_dtfc_general_.why: When assessing the controls attaching to a General Account over time, note that inactivity/dormancy is a separate status regime from freezing and applies even to compliant customers. Chapter 12 requires a DTFC to classify a General Account with no movement for one year as 'Inactive' (dual control to reactivate) and after two years as 'Dormant' (higher-authority dual control), expressly stating this 'has no relation with the rules of account freezing.' You should therefore treat dormancy and ID-expiry freezing as parallel, cumulative triggers, and check that reactivation controls exist independently of the opening/funding rules — and that a linked live Term Deposit Account pauses the inactivity clock.

clause_a.excerpt: Funds can only be withdrawn from General Account based on the instructions or agreement of the accountholder.

clause_b.excerpt: If a General Account completes an one year period with no movement whatsoever... DTFCs must consider such General Account as "Inactive" and should be subjected to dual control.

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_dtfc_general_.why: When determining how a DTFC must respond to official disclosure or blocking demands, read the operating rules together with the opening data-capture requirements, because the search obligation depends on data gathered at opening. Chapter 14 requires that all communications on disclosure/blocking pass through SAMA only, and that any search cover every category of account (active, closed, suspense, inactive, dormant), while the opening chapter fixes what customer and authorized-person data must be recorded. You should conclude that a DTFC cannot respond directly to a court or other authority — only via SAMA — and that its disclosure reply must confirm all account categories were searched.

clause_a.excerpt: DTFCs must obtain and record the following information / documents (at a minimum) before opening General Account.

clause_b.excerpt: communications between these official authorities and the DTFCs should be made through SAMA only... include... all active, closed, suspense, inactive, dormant... accounts.

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_dtfc_general_.why: When structuring a DTFC's deposit products, treat the General Account and Term Deposit Account as strictly dependent, not free-standing: a Term Deposit Account can only be opened where the same customer already holds an active General Account, and it may only be credited from — and repaid to — the General Account to which it was linked at initiation. The opening rules state the General Account's sole purpose is to facilitate Term Deposit operations, and Chapter 10 forbids de-linking and re-linking a Term Deposit Account to a different General Account. You should conclude that funds cannot circulate between unrelated customers or accounts through this pairing, and that the linkage fixed at initiation is legally binding and non-transferable.

clause_a.excerpt: the sole purpose of the General Account is to facilitate operations of Term Deposit Accounts... DTFC must credit the principle and profit amount separately to the General Account from which Term Deposit Account was funded.

clause_b.excerpt: A General Deposit Account of the same customer is already open and active... DTFCs must not de-link the Term Deposit Account with the General Account to which it was linked.

markdown_sama_en_8383_ver1_operating_rul.why: When advising a Deposit-Taking Finance Company (DTFC) on account operations, treat the General Account and Term Deposit Account rules as one integrated regime rather than separate products, because the operating rules make the General Account exist solely to service Term Deposits and hard-wire funding flows between them. Under the linkage rules a Term Deposit may only be credited from the General Account to which it was tied at initiation, must share that account's name, cannot be de-linked/re-linked, and on maturity principal and profit route back to the originating General Account. For compliance decisions, conclude that you cannot assess Term Deposit obligations (funding source matching, disclosure/blocking on SAMA request, freezing on ID expiry) in isolation — the linked General Account inherits the same customer identity and is captured in any SAMA disclosure or blocking search.

clause_a.excerpt: As stated in Section 1.1, the sole purpose of the General Account is to facilitate operations of Term Deposit Accounts.

clause_b.excerpt: DTFC must linked Term Deposit Account to a General Account upon its initiation. (Term Deposit Account will only receive credits from the same General Account to which it is linked...)

markdown_sama_en_853_ver1_aml_law||markd.why: When scoping AML/CTF obligations for a Saudi FI or DNFBP, do not treat money-laundering and terrorist-financing rules as fully separate codes, because the CTF Law's own text cross-refers to the Anti-Money Laundering Law for the monitoring standard. Article 69 requires ongoing scrutiny of transactions 'as prescribed by the relevant provisions stipulated in the Anti-Money Laundering Law,' so the CTF preventive-measures regime borrows the AML transaction-monitoring baseline. markdown_sama_en_853_ver1_aml_law||markd.why: When identifying the operative CTF duties that bind FIs, DNFBPs and NPOs, treat Chapter Six 'Preventive Measures' (Arts 63–71) as the enforceable obligation set, and note it explicitly ties back to the Anti-Money Laundering Law for the monitoring standard. The preventive-measures articles impose TF risk assessment, risk-based CDD/EDD, ten-year record-keeping, ongoing transaction scrutiny (per the AML Law), STR reporting and tipping-off prohibitions. markdown_sama_en_853_ver1_gd_financial_i.why: When determining where and how FIs, DNFBPs and NPOs must report TF suspicions, connect the Preventive Measures duty (Art 70) to the General Directorate of Financial Intelligence as the mandated recipient and analytical body (Arts 76–77). For a compliance decision, conclude that STRs go directly to the Directorate, but the tipping-off prohibition (Art 71) and the confidentiality regime constrain what may be disclosed to the customer about that reporting.

Chapter 9 grants supervisory authorities powers to inspect, compel information, and impose sanctions — written warnings, fines up to SAR 5,000,000 per violation, employment bans, management removal, and licence suspension/withdrawal — for failure to comply with 'any provision of this Law, its Implementing Regulation or relevant decisions or circulars.' markdown_sama_en_8684_ver1_basel_iii||ma.why: When calculating the countercyclical capital buffer, treat SAMA's circular as the operative KSA requirement and Basel III as the conceptual origin it invokes. markdown_sama_en_9068_ver1_hli_practices.why: When assessing how a Saudi bank must manage exposures to highly leveraged institutions or hedge funds, do not read the Basle HLI 'sound practices' paper in isolation — SAMA's transmittal expressly requires those exposures to be managed 'in accordance with the Internal Control Guidelines for Commercial Banks issued by SAMA.' That makes the HLI paper an additional, HLI-specific overlay on top of the pre-existing SAMA internal control regime and the bank's own credit policies, not a standalone or substitute framework. Conclude that both instruments apply cumulatively, and check the SAMA Internal Control Guidelines as the baseline against which HLI-specific practices are layered.

markdown_sama_en_9068_ver1_hli_practices.why: When evaluating whether a bank's counterparty credit-risk controls for HLIs meet SAMA's expectation, treat Potential Future Exposure (PFE) as a required measurement concept the sound-practices paper mandates, not an optional analytic. The paper states banks 'must have an effective measure of PFE' to convert derivatives to loan-equivalent amounts, to set binding counterparty limits, and to run stress tests under volatile conditions. markdown_sama_en_9381_ver1_bnpl_license|.why: When advising a BNPL applicant, treat these BNPL licensing guidelines as subordinate procedural instruments that derive their authority from the Finance Companies Control Law and the Rules Regulating BNPL Companies — the guidelines expressly state defined terms carry the same meaning as in that Law and Rules. markdown_sama_en_9451_ver1_new_products_.why: When determining what a bank must do before launching a new product, read the Notification and Non-Objection provisions (Section 7) as the operative gate within the New Products Regulation, and note they are not interchangeable. Notification (7.1) is the default and is only available to banks that satisfy the required maturity level in the Cyber Security, Counter-Fraud, Business Continuity and IT Governance Frameworks; non-objection (7.2) is the exception required for specified products (home loans, financial leases, derivatives, and products not covered by existing SAMA rules) and is mandatory for banks that do not meet that maturity level. Conclude that you must first classify the product and confirm the bank's framework-maturity status to know whether mere notification suffices or prior SAMA non-objection is legally required before launch.

clause_b.excerpt: Banks are required to seek SAMA's non-objection for the below products and services prior launching, as an exception to the notification requirements

markdown_sama_en_9451_ver1_new_products_.why: When determining what a bank must do before launching a new product, treat the risk-assessment requirements as an integral component of the overarching New Products Regulation, not a separate exercise. The Regulation states risks from new/modified products 'must be identified, assessed, monitored and managed appropriately by the banks,' and Section 6.3 operationalizes this by mandating a full risk assessment that 'form[s] the basis on whether or not to introduce them to the market.' A compliance reader should conclude that failing to complete and document the 6.3 risk classification and lifecycle review is itself a breach of the Regulation's core obligation, and that the risk assessment output is a prerequisite to any notification or non-objection decision.

markdown_sama_en_9451_ver1_derivatives||.why: When scoping the pre-launch approval path for a derivatives product, do not rely on the lighter notification track — financial derivatives are expressly carved into the non-objection regime. Clause 7.2.1 lists 'Financial Derivatives' among products requiring SAMA's prior non-objection 'as an exception to the notification requirements,' and Section 7.3 layers additional suitability and bona-fide-economic-purpose conditions on top. A reader should conclude that a derivative cannot be launched on acknowledgment receipt alone; the bank must obtain affirmative non-objection, launch within 12 months, and satisfy the 7.3 customer-suitability tests before offering.

clause_b.excerpt: Banks are required to seek SAMA's non-objection for the below products and services prior launching, as an exception to the notification requirements... 3. Financial Derivatives

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_operational_r.why: When mapping which operational-risk exposures require dedicated controls, note that physical-security risks are addressed by a separate detailed rule-set the Guide points to. The Guide identifies crime, robbery and burglary as operational-risk categories and records that 'the Agency has issued detailed rules in 1995 entitled "Minimum Physical Security Standards",' while the risk-reduction questionnaire tests whether programs cover 'Physical security of the bank's premises.' A reader should conclude that the Guide's high-level treatment of physical/crime exposure is supplemented by the 1995 Standards, which should be consulted for the actual physical-security requirements.

clause_a.excerpt: In recognition of these trends the Agency has issued detailed rules in 1995 entitled "Minimum Physical Security Standards"

clause_b.locator: Page 45 / Operational Risk Reduction and Control
clause_b.excerpt: do these programs include: ... Physical security of the bank's premises ?

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_operational_r.caveat: Physical-security material appears embedded within the same source document; verify the standalone 1995 Standards text for specific requirements.

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_operational_r.why: When evaluating a bank against the operational-risk expectations, use the Risk Management Evaluation Questionnaire as the assessment instrument that operationalizes the Guide's substantive concepts. The Guide defines the terms — Operational Risk, Risk Assessment and Control Matrices, the Operational Risk Management Plan — and the Questionnaire tests them directly, e.g. whether the bank can 'identify actual and potential loss exposures and risk events for all products and services' and whether 'formal written programs... including risk assessment and control matrices' exist. A reader should conclude the two are the standard-and-checklist pair: the Guide sets the definitions and expectations, the Questionnaire is the yardstick for demonstrating compliance.
