markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_criminal_risk.why: When mapping this SAMA operational-risk guidance, treat criminal risk as a sub-category of the broader operational-risk concept rather than a separate regime. The overview defines operational risk as 'pure risk' with only loss/no-loss outcomes and expressly names 'losses due to criminal activity (fraud, counterfeiting, forgery, etc.)' as examples, so criminal risk falls inside the operational-risk framework the guide addresses. For a compliance reader this means criminal-risk controls are part of the Operational Risk Management Plan approved by the Board, not an independent AML obligation, and should be assessed within that governance structure.

clause_a.excerpt: Examples of operational risk are: losses due to criminal activity (fraud, counterfeiting, forgery, etc.)

clause_b.excerpt: Operational risk - as distinct from financial risk - represents pure risk... only two possible outcomes - loss or no loss

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_counterfeit_c.why: Read counterfeit currency as one enumerated element of the guide's 'Criminal Risk' category (section 2.1), not a standalone topic. The overview lists 'counterfeiting' among operational-risk examples and section 2.1.3 addresses counterfeit currency directly, including the need for banks to 'remain vigilant.' For assessment purposes this tells you counterfeit-currency exposure is captured within the operational/criminal-risk framework the Operational Risk Management Plan must address, so any related controls sit under that plan rather than a distinct rule set.

clause_a.excerpt: despite advances in design and manufacture of currencies, counterfeiting activities will continue to increase. Consequently banks must remain vigilant

clause_b.excerpt: losses due to criminal activity (fraud, counterfeiting, forgery, etc.)

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_criminal_risk.why: Treat electronic crime as a listed sub-element of the guide's criminal-risk category (section 2.1.5), alongside fraud, forgery and counterfeiting. The index places 'Electronic Crime' under '2.1 Criminal Risks,' and the guide notes it is 'no different except for mode of execution,' with insurance (ECC) coverage discussed as a risk-transfer response. For a compliance reader, this confirms electronic-crime loss exposure is part of the operational/criminal-risk framework and should be scoped within the Operational Risk Management Plan, including any risk-transfer decisions.

clause_a.excerpt: the single largest area of operational risk within the Saudi banks has been that associated with criminal activities

clause_b.excerpt: 2.1 Criminal Risks... 2.1.5 Electronic Crime; 2.1.6 Retail Electronic Crime

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_criminal_risk.why: Forgery is expressly one of the criminal-risk sub-elements (section 2.1.2) within this operational-risk guide, not a separate compliance heading. The index nests 'Forgery' under '2.1 Criminal Risks,' and the text records it as historically the second-largest area of operational loss (~12%), tied to employee failures to verify document authenticity. For assessment this means forgery-loss controls belong to the operational/criminal-risk program the Board-approved plan must cover, and the guide flags an expected shift from simple to technically sophisticated forgeries as advances in payment systems occur.

clause_a.excerpt: financial losses attributable to fraud end other criminal activities... 100% of all operational losses claimed under existing insurance coverage

clause_b.excerpt: forgery (including check fraud) was the second largest area of operational loss, accounting for approximately 12% of total reported losses

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_criminal_risk.why: Fraud is the first and largest enumerated criminal-risk element (section 2.1.1) in this guide, so it should be scoped inside the operational/criminal-risk framework rather than treated as an isolated AML matter. The guide states criminal activity is the single largest operational-risk area and identifies fraud (predominantly employee-perpetrated, plus card, ATM and POS fraud) as the leading operational loss. For a compliance reader, this locates fraud-loss controls within the Board-approved Operational Risk Management Plan and signals particular attention to internal (employee) fraud and payment-card exposure.

clause_a.excerpt: Historically, the single largest area of operational risk within the Saudi banks has been that associated with criminal activities

clause_b.excerpt: Fraud currently represents the single largest area of operational loss within the Kingdom's banking system

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_criminal_risk.why: When assessing the operational-risk scope of this SAMA guide, treat 'Robbery and Burglary' as one enumerated sub-category of the broader 'Criminal Risk' element (section 2.1), not as a stand-alone regime. The guide lists Fraud, Forgery, Counterfeit Currency, Robbery and Burglary, and Electronic Crime as the components of criminal risk, so a reader can conclude the robbery/burglary discussion is scoped and prioritised within that taxonomy. Note the guide's own assessment that robbery/burglary is currently a low operational exposure in the Kingdom, cross-referencing the 1995 'Minimum Physical Security Standards' rules for the applicable controls.

clause_a.excerpt: 2.1 CRIMINAL RISK ... the single largest area of operational risk within the Saudi banks has been that associated with criminal activities.

clause_b.excerpt: 2.1.4 Robbery and Burglary ... the Agency has issued detailed rules in 1995 entitled "Minimum Physical Security Standards".

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_bbb_fib||mark.why: When considering how this guide expects fraud loss to be treated, note that the Bankers Blanket Bond/Financial Institution Bond is presented as the risk-transfer response to fraud, sitting alongside training, prevention/detection programmes and internal audit. The guide expressly names BBB/FIB as one control for the incidence of fraud, and the BBB/FIB's insuring agreements (employee dishonesty, etc.) map directly onto fraud exposures. A reader can conclude the two concepts are linked as risk-and-transfer, but this is guidance framing rather than a binding purchase mandate, so verify whether any separate SAMA instrument makes such cover compulsory.

clause_a.excerpt: The incidence of fraud may be controlled through ... internal auditing and, finally, through the Bankers Blanket Bond (BBB) and Financial Institution Bond (FIB).

clause_b.excerpt: Fraud currently represents the single largest area of operational loss within the Kingdom's banking system.

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_bbb_fib||mark.caveat: Relation is 'conceptually_related_to'; the guide describes BBB/FIB as one option among controls, not a mandated requirement — confirm against any binding SAMA rule before relying on it.

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_ecc_coverage|.why: When mapping insurance coverage to the electronic-crime risk category, note that ECC coverage is the guide's designated risk-transfer response to third-party fraud affecting computer and telecommunications systems. Importantly, the guide states ECC 'may not be written without a BBB/FIB being present' and is treated as a companion piece purchased in the same limit, so a reader should conclude the two coverages are dependent, not free-standing. Treat this as guidance describing market coverage structure rather than a SAMA mandate to buy either.

clause_a.excerpt: the ECC coverage may not be written without a BBB/FIB being present ... it is truly a companion piece to the BBB/FIB.

clause_b.excerpt: 2.1.5 Electronic Crime ... no different except for mode of execution

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_ecc_coverage|.caveat: Relation is 'conceptually_related_to' and describes insurance-market structure; the electronic-crime node text is truncated, so confirm the substantive risk description before relying on the mapping.

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_do_liability|.why: When scoping professional-risk exposure under this guide, treat Directors and Officers liability as a distinct branch of 'Professional Risk' that attaches to the individuals (board and officers) rather than the bank itself. The guide separates D&O (broad in wrongful acts, narrow in persons covered) from Professional Indemnity (narrow to specific bank services), so a reader should not conflate the two when assessing who bears exposure or which cover responds. The guide flags that substantial D&O exposure already exists for Kingdom banks and escalates for those operating in foreign jurisdictions.

clause_a.excerpt: This coverage is for the directors and officer of a bank, and not for the bank itself ... The personal assets of directors and senior officers may be at risk

clause_b.excerpt: 2.2. Professional Risk ... currently constitute both the single largest and most rapidly growing form of operational risk

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_professional_.why: When identifying which coverage responds to the bank's own professional-risk exposure, treat Professional Indemnity as the branch of 'Professional Risk' that indemnifies the bank itself against third-party claims for errors, omissions or imprudence by its directors, officers and employees. The guide distinguishes PI (covering only specific professional services — trust, brokerage, investment advisory) from D&O, so a reader should conclude PI is narrower in the acts covered and does not substitute for D&O. This informs how to allocate the bank-level versus individual-level slices of professional liability.

clause_a.excerpt: Professional Indemnity ... designed to indemnify the bank itself against litigation by customers, and other third parties alleging errors, omissions ...

clause_b.excerpt: Exposures directly related to the provision of financial products and services currently constitute ... the single largest ... form of operational risk

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_finite_risk_i.why: When assessing whether a bank's operational-risk financing policy is complete under this SAMA inspection guidance, treat finite risk insurance and self insurance as complementary components of a single risk-financing continuum rather than substitutes. The guide expressly defines finite risk insurance as an approach that 'involve risk transfer through regular insurance and self insurance,' so a compliant risk financing policy should address both together. You would check that the bank's Board-approved policy documents loss retention guidelines and finite programs jointly, not rely on one label to satisfy the other.

clause_a.excerpt: the finite risk insurance approach. This approach involve risk transfer through regular insurance and self insurance, and generally has an upper l...

clause_b.excerpt: The various forms of insurance schemes include self insurance, regular insurance and other insurance alternatives

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_finite_risk_i.why: When mapping which risk-financing options a bank must analyze, note that finite risk insurance is not a standalone alternative to conventional/regular insurance but a hybrid that draws on it. The guide states the finite approach 'involve risk transfer through regular insurance and self insurance,' meaning regular insurance is a building block within a finite program. In reviewing a bank's risk financing policy you would expect coverage decisions on finite programs to be evaluated alongside, not in isolation from, its conventional insurance placements.

clause_a.excerpt: the finite risk insurance approach. This approach involve risk transfer through regular insurance and self insurance

clause_b.excerpt: forms of insurance schemes include self insurance, regular insurance and other insurance alternatives

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_deductibles||.why: When examining a bank's conventional (regular) insurance program, treat deductibles/retention levels as an integral parameter of that program, not a separate topic. The guide places Deductibles (3.2.3) within the 'Regular Insurance' section (3.2) and links them directly to specific covers such as employee-infidelity coverage under the BBB/FIB, illustrating that deductible structure is set relative to the underlying regular insurance policy. In assessing coverage adequacy you would verify that straight and aggregate deductibles are calibrated against the retained-risk appetite documented in the loss retention guidelines rather than treated as merely a pricing detail.

clause_a.excerpt: deductibles should be used to eliminate coverage for losses that are apt to occur with some degree of regularity... employee infidelity coverage under the BBB/FIB

clause_b.excerpt: 3.2 Regular Insurance ... 3.2.3 Deductibles

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_bbb_fib||mark.why: When reviewing a bank's crime/fidelity insurance program, do not treat ECC coverage as freely purchasable on its own: the guide states 'ECC coverage may not be written without a BBB/FIB being present,' making the Bankers Blanket Bond/Financial Institution Bond a precondition for ECC. Both are listed among the six primary coverage types under Regular Insurance, and ECC is described as a 'companion piece' generally purchased in the same limit as the BBB/FIB. In assessing coverage completeness you would confirm a BBB/FIB is in force before crediting the bank with ECC protection and would expect their limits to be aligned.

clause_a.excerpt: TheBankers Blanket Bond/Financial Institution Bond (BBB/FIB)- This coverage generally consists of six basic insuring agreements

clause_b.excerpt: ECC coverage may not be written without a BBB/FIB being present ... it is truly a companion piece to the BBB/FIB

markdown_sama_en_9492_ver1_operational_r.why: When evaluating a bank's operational-risk governance structure against this guidance, treat the Operational Risk Management Committee and the Operational Risk Manager as a defined reporting hierarchy, not interchangeable functions. The glossary defines the Committee as 'reporting directly to the Operational Risk Manager,' and the Manager as the senior person responsible for developing and implementing the plan and reporting to the Managing Director/General Manager. The two also jointly develop the Operational Risk Management Plan for Board approval, so you would check that both roles exist, that the reporting lines run Committee → Manager → MD/GM, and that plan ownership is not left ambiguous.

clause_a.excerpt: Operational Risk Management Committee - An operational committee of the bank reporting directly to the Operational Risk Manager

clause_b.excerpt: Operational Risk Manager - The senior manager ... responsible for the development of the bank's Operational Risk Management Plan ... should report directly to the managing Director/General Manager

markdown_sama_en_9538_ver1_aer||markdown.why: When applying the Savings Products Rules to a bank's deposit products, treat AER as a rule-defined term, not a marketing figure: the Rules' definitions article expressly ties the customer's return to the annual equivalent rate and points to SAMA's separate Disclosure of Rates rules for how AER is computed. This means AER disclosures in savings products must be consistent with that cross-referenced disclosure regime, so you cannot assess advertising/disclosure compliance under these Rules in isolation. Check the referenced Disclosure of Financing and Savings Product Prices rules for the binding AER calculation methodology before signing off.

clause_a.excerpt: العائد الربح على مبلغ الإيداع محسوباً وفق المعدل السنوي المكافئ (AER) ... وفق الموضح في قواعد الإفصاح عن أسعار المنتجات التمويلية والادخارية

clause_b.excerpt: General Rules for Savings Products in Banks ... Saudi Central Bank

markdown_sama_en_9538_ver1_aer||markdown.caveat: Source Arabic is partly OCR-garbled; AER methodology lives in the separately-issued disclosure rules, which should be consulted directly.

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_basel_framewo.why: When determining capital adequacy for a Shari'ah-compliant bank, do not read this Additional Requirements document as a self-contained regime: it is expressly subordinate to and must be read alongside SAMA's Basel framework (circular no. 44047144, 28 Dec 2022, and subsequent updates), supplying only mapping rules for Islamic products. RWA calculations for credit and market risk still follow the Basel framework, while this document tells you which stage of each Islamic contract attracts credit vs market risk weighting. Conclude that both instruments must be applied together, and always use the current Basel framework version since these additions defer to it.

clause_a.excerpt: which are to be read alongside the applicable SAMA's Basel framework issued via circular no. 44047144 dated 04-06-1444AH ... and any subsequent updates

clause_b.excerpt: Calculations for risk weighted assets (RWAs) ... are to follow the prudential treatment as per the applicable SAMA's Basel framework

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_ijarah||markd.why: When capital-weighting a lease-based Islamic exposure, use this document's Ijarah definition and its stage tables (Operating Ijarah 5J, Ijarah Muntahia Bi Al Tamlik 5K) to decide when credit vs market risk applies across the contract lifecycle. Critically, note the carve-out: Table 5K does not apply to real estate finance exposures, which continue under the existing SAMA Basel methodology. Conclude that Ijarah treatment is stage-dependent and asset-type-dependent, so verify whether your exposure is real-estate finance before applying these tables.

clause_a.excerpt: Table 5K does not apply to real estate finance exposures. All ijarah structured real estate finance exposures shall continue using the methodology ... in the existing SAMA Basel framework

clause_b.excerpt: additional requirements for mapping Shari'ah compliant assets to SAMA's Basel framework ... through the various stages of the contract

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_istisna||mark.why: When weighting Istisna' exposures, this document distinguishes several sub-cases that carry different risk weights: with vs without Parallel Istisna', and project-finance variants (Tables 5F–5I). The defined term Istisna' (and Parallel Istisna') governs which table applies, and stages such as 'unbilled work-in-process inventory' vs 'amounts receivable after contract billings' switch between market-risk and credit-risk weighting. Conclude that you must first classify the exact Istisna' structure and contract stage, since a mis-classification (e.g. treating a non-parallel istisna' as parallel) changes the applicable capital charge.

clause_a.excerpt: Istisna: The sale of a specified asset, with an obligation on the part of the seller to manufacture/construct it ... to be paid in one lump sum or instalments

clause_b.excerpt: This section provides additional requirements for mapping Shari'ah compliant assets to SAMA's Basel framework, given their structure ... through the various stages of the contract

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_mudarabah||ma.why: When capital-treating a Mudarabah position, note that this document classifies it as an equity exposure rather than routing it through the contract-stage credit/market tables: Musharakah/Mudarabah/Wakalah are weighted under the equity and transition arrangements of SAMA's Basel framework. The defined term Mudarabah (partnership where losses fall on the capital provider absent misconduct) supports that equity characterisation. Conclude that Mudarabah RWAs are determined by the Basel equity treatment, not the murabahah/istisna-style stage tables, so apply the correct branch of the framework.

clause_a.excerpt: Banks are required to calculate risk weights assets for equity exposure (i.e. Musharakah/Mudarabah/Wakalah) in accordance to the treatment of equity ... in SAMA's Basel framework

clause_b.excerpt: Mudarabah: A partnership contract between the capital provider (rabb al-mal) and an entrepreneur (mudarib) ... losses are to be borne solely by the capital provider

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_murabahah||ma.why: When determining the capital treatment of a Murabahah exposure, treat the Murabahah definition and the capital-adequacy instrument as a single reading: the defined contract stages drive whether a credit or market risk-weight applies. The document defines Murabahah and then, in Tables 5A/5B, prescribes stage-specific treatment — before sale the asset attracts market risk (non-binding) or credit risk (binding); after sale/transfer the receivable attracts credit risk. You should conclude the binding vs non-binding purchase order distinction in the definition is dispositive for which capital charge the bank must hold, and check which stage a given exposure sits at before assigning a risk-weight.

clause_a.excerpt: Murabahah: A sale contract whereby the bank sells to a customer a specified asset, whereby the selling price is the sum of the cost price and an agreed profit margin.

clause_b.excerpt: Table 5A: Murabahah and non-binding purchase order... Table 5B: Murabahah and binding purchase order

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_musharakah||m.why: When scoping capital treatment for a Musharakah position, do not map it to the contract-stage tables used for sale/lease products; the instrument routes Musharakah through the equity-exposure regime instead. The document defines Musharakah as a capital-contribution partnership and then, in Section 6, requires banks to risk-weight Musharakah/Mudarabah/Wakalah 'in accordance to the treatment of equity and transition arrangements in SAMA's Basel framework.' You should conclude that equity-exposure rules and transition arrangements — not the murabahah/salam/istisna tables — govern these positions, and verify which Basel equity treatment applies.

clause_a.excerpt: Musharakah: A partnership contract in which the partners agree to contribute capital to an enterprise, whether existing or new.

clause_b.excerpt: Banks are required to calculate risk weights assets for equity exposure (i.e. Musharakah/Mudarabah/Wakalah) in accordance to the treatment of equity and transition arrangements in SAMA's Basel framework.

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_salam||markdo.why: When assessing capital held against a Salam exposure, use the defined contract structure together with the stage tables, because whether a Parallel Salam exists changes the treatment. The document defines Salam and Parallel Salam and then splits treatment across Table 5D (with Parallel Salam) and Table 5E (without) — at payment of purchase price both credit and market risk-weights apply, while receipt of the commodity is N/A for credit risk. You should conclude the presence or absence of a matched Parallel Salam and the contract stage both determine the charge, and confirm which table governs before assigning a risk-weight.

clause_a.excerpt: Salam: The sale of a specified commodity that is of a known type, quantity and attributes for a known price paid at the time of signing the contract for its delivery in the future

clause_b.excerpt: Table 5D: Salam with Parallel Salam... Table 5E: Salam without Parallel Salam... Payment of purchase price by the bank to a salam customer/seller — Refer to Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_shariah_capit.why: When determining the capital charge for a Tawarruq/CMT, note the treatment turns on whether there is a binding purchase promise and enforceable documentation. The document defines CMT as a liquidity-generating commodity murabahah and Table 5C provides that with a binding promise and legally enforceable documentation there is no market-risk charge, whereas absent that promise commodities on balance sheet attract market risk and delivered commodities attract credit risk. You should conclude that the legal enforceability of the counterparty's purchase undertaking directly reduces the capital requirement, and verify the documentation actually meets the enforceability condition before relying on the nil charge.

clause_a.excerpt: In the presence of a binding promise from the counterparty to purchase, and legally enforceable contract documentation, there will be no capital charge for market risk

clause_b.excerpt: Tawarruq or Commodity Murabahah Transaction (CMT): A murabahah transaction based on the purchase of a commodity... for the purpose of obtaining liquidity, provided that there are no links between the two contracts.

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_credit_risk||.why: When a Murabahah asset has been sold and the selling price is receivable from the customer, treat it as a credit-risk exposure and apply SAMA's Basel Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk. The tables link the Murabahah contract stage directly to the credit-risk regime: once title transfers and a receivable is due (Table 5A) or upon delivery under a binding order (Table 5B), the credit risk-weight applies. You should conclude that the credit-risk capital rules are the operative reference for the receivable leg of a Murabahah, and confirm the contract stage rather than assuming a single treatment across the transaction's life.

clause_a.excerpt: Refer to Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk

clause_b.excerpt: Asset is sold and title is transferred to a customer, and the selling price (accounts receivable) is due from the customer — Refer to Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_market_risk||.why: When determining capital adequacy for a Shari'ah-compliant Salam exposure, you cannot treat market risk in isolation — the SAMA framework assigns market-risk capital by contract stage. For a Salam contract (with or without Parallel Salam), the tables direct that at the stage of price payment by the bank, both credit-risk and market-risk minimum capital requirements apply, while receipt of the commodity carries N/A. Conclude that the applicable market-risk charge for Salam depends on the specific stage in Tables 5D/5E, so map each contract phase to the correct treatment rather than applying a single blanket weight.

clause_a.excerpt: Payment of purchase price by the bank to a salam customer/seller ... Refer to Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk

clause_b.excerpt: Salam: The sale of a specified commodity ... for a known price paid at the time of signing the contract for its delivery in the future

markdown_sama_en_9618_ver1_ijarah||markd.why: When scoping capital treatment for Ijarah (operating lease and Ijarah Muntahia Bi Al Tamlik), check the market-risk column stage-by-stage, because the framework attaches market-risk capital primarily where the leased asset sits on the bank's books without a binding lease and where the asset is returned at maturity. Tables 5J and 5K show market-risk requirements apply pre-lease and on return, while credit-risk applies once a binding lease/rental is due. Note the carve-out: Table 5K expressly excludes real estate finance exposures, which stay under the existing SAMA Basel methodology — so verify the asset type before selecting the treatment.

clause_a.excerpt: (1) Table 5K does not apply to real estate finance exposures. All ijarah structured real estate finance exposures shall continue using the methodology ... in the existing SAMA Basel framework

clause_b.excerpt: Asset available for lease (prior to signing a lease contract) without binding lease agreement ... Refer to Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk

markdown_sama_en_961_ver1_credit_informa.why: When assessing who is authorised to operate as a credit bureau in KSA, treat 'Companies' as a defined status created and constrained by this Law, not a generic label. Article 1 defines credit information companies as entities 'licensed to collect and maintain credit information ... and provide the same to members,' and Article 12 makes operating without a SAMA licence a violation. Conclude that any entity collecting/exchanging consumer credit data must hold a SAMA licence and that the Law's confidentiality, accuracy and consumer-consent obligations attach to that licensed status.

clause_a.excerpt: Companies: Credit information companies licensed to collect and maintain credit information on consumers and provide the same to members upon request

clause_b.excerpt: engaging in activities of credit information companies without obtaining a license from SAMA

markdown_sama_en_961_ver1_credit_informa.why: When advising on consumer rights over their credit data, anchor them in the Law's defined 'Credit Record' — a report issued by companies containing consumer credit information — because that definition triggers the Article 9 rights (consent to establish, free copy on decline, right to annotate, right to correct errors and escalate to the committee). The Law also imposes maintenance duties on companies under Article 10. Conclude that any dispute over record accuracy, access fees, or unlawful requests is governed by these statutory rights and the committee mechanism, not by contract alone.

clause_a.excerpt: Credit Record: A report issued by companies containing consumer credit information

clause_b.excerpt: A consumer credit record may not be established with companies for the first time except with the written consent of the consumer

markdown_sama_en_961_ver1_credit_informa.why: When determining the full compliance perimeter under the Credit Information Law, do not rely on the primary Law alone — it repeatedly delegates operative detail (fees, update timelines, retention periods, committee mechanics, licensing controls) to the Implementing Regulations, which SAMA's Governor must issue within 180 days and publish in the Official Gazette. Article 12 further makes breach of the Implementing Regulations itself a violation carrying Article 13 penalties (fines up to one million riyals, suspension, or licence revocation). Conclude that any assessment of update-timing or retention obligations must be verified against the current Implementing Regulations, not just the Law's articles.

clause_a.excerpt: The Governor of SAMA shall issue the Implementing Regulations of this Law within (180) days ... and ... shall be published in the Official Gazette

clause_b.excerpt: any other violation of the provisions of this Law or its Implementing Regulations ... a fine not exceeding one million riyals

markdown_sama_en_961_ver1_credit_informa.why: When assessing a licensed credit bureau's obligations under the Credit Information Law, treat 'Credit Record' as the defined output that 'Companies' are legally required to produce, maintain and exchange — the two terms are locked together by Article 1's definitions and Article 4(3). This means a credit information company's core statutory duties (accuracy, first-time consumer consent under Article 9, error correction, retention under Article 10) all attach to the credit record it issues; you cannot scope the company's liability without reference to the record. Conclude that any compliance review of the company must test the record's lifecycle — consent, accuracy, correction, retention and confidentiality — as inseparable duties.

clause_a.excerpt: Companies: Credit information companies licensed to collect and maintain credit information on consumers and provide the same to members upon request.

clause_b.excerpt: Credit Record: A report issued by companies containing consumer credit information.

markdown_sama_en_9660_ver1_qr_code_payme.why: These two circulars appear to connect only as parallel components of SAMA's payments-oversight regime — one on QR Code payment technology, the other on a unified pricing model for POS and e-commerce mada transactions — rather than through any cross-reference between them. Both derive from SAMA's exclusive authority over payment systems in the Kingdom, so they share a regulatory parent but govern different subject matter (technical/interoperability standards vs. merchant pricing). Before relying on any link, verify the primary texts: there is no evidence in the provided context that the QR project imports or amends the pricing model, so treat them as separate obligations and do not assume compliance with one satisfies the other.

clause_a.excerpt: مشروع تطوير ... المدفوعات من خلال تقنية رمز الاستجابة السريع (QR Code) ... تعزيز ... توافقية نظم المدفوعات

0.theme: Operational resilience regime for data-aggregation providers: business continuity and cyber-security obligations that SAMA imposes on regulated entities, anchored in the Instructions for Practicing Aggregation Activity and the BCM/Cyber frameworks they incorporate.
how_members_connect: The Aggregation Instructions cite the SAMA BCM Framework and Cyber Security Framework, making those framework controls (BCP, DRP, BIA/risk assessment, crisis management, cyber resilience) enforceable requirements on the Aggregation Entity.

Hierarchy runs from SAMA-owned frameworks (BCM, CSF) down to obligations 'implemented by' each Member Organization; CRFR further decomposes cyber duties into governance, operations/technology and resilience domains.
Defined-actor chain: Aggregation Entity is the obligated party serving the Consumer and interfacing with Financier via the Aggregation Platform; SAMA is supervisor and framework owner.
External standards (ISO 22301, NISTIR 7298, PCI-DSS, SWIFT CSCF) are cited as benchmarks the SAMA frameworks map to, not as independent obligations.

1.theme: Bank prudential regime under the Banking Control Law and Basel III: concentration-risk (large exposures), capital adequacy (ICAAP/Pillar 1&2) and liquidity (LCR/HQLA) rules that bind licensed banks.
how_members_connect: The LEX Rules cite the Banking Control Law and Basel III capital framework as their legal/standard-setting basis, then reference operative concepts — Maximum Exposure Limits, Group of Connected Counterparties, exposure-value definition, SA-CCR, LTA, QCCP treatment.
LCR guidance (SAMA General/Specific Guidance) cites the Basel III LCR standards and cascades into HQLA tiers (Level 1/2/2B), inflow/outflow run-off categories and monitoring tools.
ICAAP/Pillar 2 links Basel II supervisory-review and stress-testing obligations to the capital adequacy assessment banks must perform.
Cross-regime overlap: Covered Bonds and Level 2 assets appear in both the LEX and LCR contexts, and 'Treatment for Shariah' flags Shariah-compliant adaptation of these prudential measures.

2.theme: AML/CTF preventive-measures regime plus the fit-and-proper gatekeeping and adjacent prudential rules for finance companies/DTFCs; covers who must apply CDD, report to the FIU, and hold approved senior positions.
how_members_connect: The AML Law is the parent statute; its Implementing Regulation, Preventive Measures for FIs/DNFBPs, Due Diligence Measures and the FIU/GDFI enforcement bodies are subordinate references defining obligations and offences (e.g. Article 2 ML offence).
The CFT Law parallels the AML Law with its own preventive measures (adding NPOs) and the Permanent Committee — a linked but distinct sanctions/TFS-adjacent regime.

Fit-and-proper chain: Requirements for Senior Appointments -> Fit and Proper Criteria -> positions needing SAMA non-objection, including the AML/CTF Director, tying governance approval to the AML function.

KYC is treated as conceptually equivalent to Due Diligence Measures; the DTFC/Finance Companies rules and IFRS 9 provisioning cluster here because account-opening/KYC and juristic-person verification bridge AML CDD and prudential asset-quality duties.

3.theme: Consumer-protection and conduct regime for finance companies, real-estate finance and banks — advertising, contracting, responsible lending, governance, outsourcing and beneficial-owner verification obligations, sitting under the core enabling laws.
how_members_connect: Foundational laws (SAMA Central Bank Law M/36, Finance Companies Control Law M/51, Real Estate Finance Law, Banking Control Law M/5) are cited as the legal basis for the operational instructions and rules above them.

Conduct instruments (Responsible Retail Financing, Advertising Controls, Consumer Protection Principles, Customer Signature on All Contract Pages, disability-services, SAMA-logo prohibition) reference Financial Institution Customer Protection as their shared obligation set.

Beneficial-owner verification instruments (Waathiq integration, nonprofit inquiry service) cross-reference the AML Law and BO Verification — a cross-regime link between consumer-facing onboarding and AML/CTF KYB duties.

Real-estate refinance rules cite both the Real Estate Finance Law and Finance Companies Control Law and pull in Outsourcing Rules and Main Governance Principles, showing the layered law -> regulation -> instruction hierarchy; scope carve-outs (optional compliance for SME/large-enterprise dealings) limit where consumer protections apply.

4.theme: Non-bank finance company regime under SAMA: finance leasing (Ijara) and its standard contracts, the contract registry, BNPL, bancassurance, and the Shariah/governance controls that overlay these licensed activities. Covers who may conduct finance-company activity and the mandatory terms of consumer finance and lease contracts.
how_members_connect: Two parent laws anchor the cluster: Finance Companies Control Law (M/51) with its Implementing Regulation licenses and supervises the companies, while Finance Lease Law (M/48) and its Executive Regulation govern the lease product itself and the Contract Registry (Sijil) — subordinate decisions (Registrar powers, General Committee formation) sit beneath M/51.

Contract-level nodes (Ijara contract, Acceptance Certificate, Loss/Insurance/Maintenance provisions, assignment/secondary market, Ownership Transfer) derive their mandatory content from the Finance Lease Law/Executive Regulation and register in the Sijil al-Uqud.

Shariah Governance Instructions cite M/51 and its Implementing Regulation, imposing Board, Shariah Committee and Shariah oversight duties on finance companies — a governance layer applying across lease and BNPL activity.

Consumer-facing rules (Consumer Finance Controls, Standard Vehicle Lease Contract, Early Repayment Guideline using Declining Balance, default/termination) cite the finance-company framework; note BNPL and bancassurance are separately scoped activities cross-referencing M/51, M/5 and M/32 respectively — distinct licensing regimes clustered by shared supervisor.

5.theme: Basel-based Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) credit risk capital regime as adopted by SAMA: how banks using internal models compute RWA, plus the credit risk mitigation (CRM) rules that reduce exposure, and the minimum requirements/validation gating IRB use.
how_members_connect: IRB risk components (PD, LGD, EAD, M) feed the risk-weight functions; asset-class taxonomy (corporate, specialized lending sub-types PF/OF/CF/IPRE/HVCRE, retail/QRRE, equity, purchased receivables) determines which function and whether F-IRB or A-IRB applies.
Specialized Lending links to the Supervisory Slotting Approach as the fallback where banks cannot estimate own parameters — a scope/exception relationship within IRB.

CRM sub-cluster (Comprehensive vs Simple collateral approach, supervisory haircuts Table 14, holding periods Table 15, Hfx currency mismatch, netting, guarantees/derivatives, sovereign guarantees) modifies LGD/EAD inputs — CRM effects are cross-referenced into the IRB risk components.

Minimum-requirement nodes (rating system design, PD estimation, Definition of Default, re-ageing, validation, disclosure) are conditions precedent to IRB eligibility, binding the modelling nodes to supervisory approval standards.

6.theme: SAMA Pillar 3 standardized disclosure templates and their governing frameworks — capital composition/TLAC, counterparty credit risk, market risk, CVA, leverage, countercyclical buffer and RWA overview. Defines mandatory public disclosure format for banks.
how_members_connect: Framework documents (SACAP capital reforms, SCCR counterparty credit risk, SMAR market risk, SLEV leverage) are the parent standards that each family of templates references and operationalizes.

Capital-composition templates interlock: CC1 reconciles to CC2 and the balance sheet, feeds KM1 key metrics, and links to PV1, TLAC1 and CDC — a chain tying regulatory capital definition to disclosed figures.

CCR templates (CCR1/3/4/5/8) all reference SCCR and cross-link (e.g. central counterparty exposures in CCR8); MR and CVA templates similarly map to SMAR and the CVA approaches, each template scoped to a specific calculation approach.
CMS templates compare modelled vs standardised RWA and tie into OV1's RWA overview, connecting IRB output back to the disclosure regime.

7.theme: Basel III liquidity regime as implemented by SAMA: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), its HQLA stock and stressed net cash-flow denominator, the NSFR, and supplementary monitoring tools — defining minimum liquidity holdings for banks.
how_members_connect: LCR is the organizing obligation: it draws HQLA (numerator) and Total Net Cash Outflows (denominator = Cash Outflows less capped Cash Inflows), and cites the Basel III/II frameworks and the BCBS Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management as parent standards.
HQLA is defined by tiering into Level 1/2A/2B assets, with Level 2B further conditioned by LTV — a definition/scope hierarchy.
Cash-outflow categories (retail/wholesale/secured run-off, operational deposits) specify the assumed stress rates that populate the denominator.

Alternative Liquidity Approaches (ALA Options 1–3, with peer-review requirement) are conditional exceptions for jurisdictions/currencies short of HQLA, and the Shari'ah-compliant bank treatment adapts HQLA eligibility — both scope-modifying links to the core LCR; NSFR sits as the complementary structural-funding measure.

8.theme: SAMA Cyber Security Framework regime: mandatory cyber-security governance, risk management, operations, and third-party controls that SAMA-regulated financial institutions must implement, with maturity-based assessment. Covers the governance/risk regime as applied to cyber resilience.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: SAMA issues the Framework as the binding parent; the Framework references its four control domains (Leadership & Governance, Risk Management & Compliance, Operations & Technology, Third Party) which subordinate the detailed obligations.

Governance obligation chain: Leadership & Governance mandates a Cyber Security Strategy, Policy, defined Roles/Responsibilities, a CISO, a Cyber Security Committee, and Board oversight — allocating accountability for enforceable requirements.

Cross-references to external standards (PCI-DSS, SWIFT CSCF, (inter)national industry standards) fold third-party benchmarks into the compliance obligation; the Glossary fixes defined terms (Vulnerability, IoC, Hard/Soft Token).

Operations domain scopes concrete control areas — incident/event/threat/vulnerability management, e-banking and payment-system security, SOC, MFA — and Third Party/Cloud provisions extend obligations to outsourced arrangements.

9.theme: Market risk capital regime: the standardised measurement of trading-book risk, spanning the Sensitivities-Based Method (SBM), the Simplified Standardised Approach, and legacy maturity/duration and options methods. Defines how banks quantify capital charges for market risk.
how_members_connect: SBM is the organizing parent, decomposing risk into Delta, Vega and Curvature and referencing the risk classes (GIRR, CSR, Equity, Commodity, FX) to which those sensitivities apply.
Sensitivity definitions chain into risk classes: PV01 measures GIRR delta, CS01 measures CSR delta; CSR further references the Correlation Trading Portfolio special treatment.

The Simplified Standardised Approach is an alternative regime referencing simplified interest-rate/commodities/equity/FX treatments and the Maturity/Duration methods, splitting Specific vs General Market Risk.
Options treatment is scoped via the Simplified Approach, Delta-plus Method and Scenario Approach, with Gamma/Vega and Supervisory Delta adjustments defining the capture of non-linear risk.

10.theme: Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) credit-risk capital regime: the minimum qualifying requirements, rating-system and risk-quantification standards, default/expected-loss and provisions treatment, and collateral recognition banks must satisfy to use internal estimates.
how_members_connect: 'Minimum Requirements to Use IRB Approach' is the gatekeeping parent referencing all qualifying conditions: rating system design, use of ratings, risk quantification, governance/control unit, validation and disclosure — permission to use IRB is conditional on all being met.

Risk Quantification chains into the estimation obligations (Definition of Default, PD/Own-LGD/Own-EAD estimation, supervisory LGD/EAD fallbacks) and the recognition of guarantees, credit derivatives and eligible collateral.

Expected-loss/provisions branch links Treatment of EL and Provisions to Calculation of EL, Total Eligible Provisions and the specialized-lending slotting EL, connecting capital treatment to accounting provisions.
Supervisory Slotting parent scopes specialized-lending sub-criteria (project, object, commodities, IPRE/HVCRE finance) as a defined alternative to own estimates.

11.theme: Securitization capital regime: classification of securitization structures, the hierarchy of capital approaches, operational requirements for risk transference, and criteria (including STC) determining preferential treatment. Governs how banks assign capital to securitization exposures.
how_members_connect: Securitization General Provisions is the definitional anchor referenced by the structure types (Traditional, Synthetic, Resecuritization) that determine which regime applies.

Hierarchy of Securitization Approaches orders the calculation methods (SEC-IRBA, SEC-ERBA, SEC-IAA, SEC-SA), with SEC-ERBA/SEC-IAA depending on ECAI ratings and KIRB/KSA charges and parameters (attachment/detachment points, supervisory p) feeding the formulas.

Operational Requirements for Risk Transference reference the SPE, clean-up calls and early-amortization provisions — the conditions a bank must meet to derecognise securitized exposures for capital purposes.
STC Securitization Criteria scope preferential treatment for STC-compliant/traditional/ABCP structures; caps, CRM and NPL/purchase-price-discount rules bound the resulting capital charge.

12.theme: Basel III / SAMA Pillar 3 public disclosure templates for regulatory capital, RWA, leverage, liquidity, market/counterparty/credit and securitisation risk. Compliance relevance: these define the mandatory content and format of prudential disclosures banks must publish to SAMA and the market.
how_members_connect: KM1 (Key Metrics) is the hub: it aggregates and cross-references the composition (CC1), liquidity (LIQ1/LIQ2), leverage (LR2) and RWA overview (OV1) figures, so consistency across templates is a compliance obligation.
OV1 (Overview of RWA) is the second hub, reconciling each risk-type template (CR, CCR, SEC, MR, CVA, CMS) into the total RWA that drives capital ratios.
Reconciliation chain (LIA -> LI1 -> LI2 -> PV1) links accounting statements to regulatory exposures, evidencing why disclosed regulatory values differ from carrying values.
TLAC-specific templates (KM2, TLAC1) apply only to G-SIB scope, a limiting condition distinct from the general capital templates.

13.theme: Basel III securitisation capital framework as adopted by SAMA: the ranked methods for computing RWA/capital on securitisation and resecuritisation exposures, plus the STC preferential-treatment regime. Relevance: dictates which capital approach a bank must apply and the eligibility gates for lower charges.
how_members_connect: The Hierarchy of Approaches sets a mandatory ordering (SEC-IRBA -> SEC-IAA/SEC-ERBA -> SEC-SA), so approach selection is a rule-driven determination, not a free choice.
SEC-IRBA is the calculation core, drawing on KIRB, attachment/detachment points and supervisory parameter p; caps and look-through provisions bound the result.

STC Framework (term and ABCP criteria) is an eligibility overlay unlocking preferential parameters only where all conditions are met; resecuritisation and NPL securitisation are carved-out stricter cases.
SAMA Circular 341000015689 is the parent adoption instrument for Basel III capital, and BCS 242 (ECAI mapping) is cited as the external-rating-to-risk-weight bridge feeding these approaches.

14.theme: KSA licensing and contractual regime for finance/refinance and real-estate mortgage lending — the statutory laws, licensing rules, and mandated contract/notice templates governing finance companies and mortgage registration.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from primary laws (Finance Companies Control Law, Real Estate Finance Law, Finance Lease Law, Registered Real Estate Mortgage Law) down to licensing guidelines/rules and prescribed contract templates.
Licensing guidelines reference common gatekeeping instruments (Fit and Proper Form, LEI/GLEIF), tying market entry to fitness and legal-entity identification requirements.

Murabaha/Ijarah contract templates operationalise the finance laws and mortgage registration into borrower-facing terms — pricing (SAIBOR index, APR), default/delay notices, late-payment and termination provisions.
Consumer-protection and credit-reporting touchpoints (notice articles, Credit Information Company) attach obligations at the borrower-relationship level within the finance-company regime.

15.theme: SAMA Counter-Fraud Framework: a supervisory framework imposing on regulated entities a structured fraud-risk regime organised into Governance, Prevent, Detect and Respond domains, assessed against a maturity model.
how_members_connect: SAMA is the issuing authority; the Framework is the parent instrument that decomposes into the four domains and is benchmarked by the Counter-Fraud Maturity Model.
Governance Domain establishes accountable structures (Committee, Department, Head, Strategy, Policy) — i.e., the who-is-responsible obligations.

Prevent/Detect/Respond domains assign operational duties (due diligence, authentication, risk assessment; detection and whistle-blowing; investigation, remediation, response planning and supervisory notification to SAMA).
Cross-references to the Cyber Security and IT Governance Frameworks show fraud controls interlock with adjacent SAMA operational-resilience regimes rather than standing alone.

16.theme: A mixed licensing-and-conduct cluster spanning bank remittance-center AML/CFT obligations, bank/digital-bank licensing and governance, and the real-estate finance/refinance regime. The common thread is SAMA-authorized activity: who may operate, under what fit-and-proper/governance conditions, and what CDD/consumer-protection duties attach.
how_members_connect: The Remittance Centers Guide is subordinate to the Banking Control Law and operationalizes AML/CFT Rules, CDD Measures, KYC, SAFIU reporting and FATF standards — a guide-level layer on top of the AML regime.

Licensing Guidelines (and the digital-only bank add-on) sit under the Banking Control Law and cross-reference Corporate Governance Principles, the Cyber Security Framework, and Fit-and-Proper/senior-appointment requirements as licensing preconditions.

A distinct real-estate finance sub-chain: Real Estate Finance Law -> its Implementing Regulation -> Rules Governing Real Estate Refinance Companies / SRC, plus Responsible Lending and Deductible Ratio consumer limits.

Finance Companies Control Law anchors outsourcing rules, material-function definitions, and compliance-manager certification for the finance-company side — read these as separate obligation stacks that happen to co-cluster, not one unified regime.

17.theme: Basel III-derived prudential capital and stress-testing regime for banks: computing operational-risk capital under the Standardized Approach and testing capital resilience through SAMA's stress-testing and ICAAP requirements, with Pillar 3 disclosure of the inputs.
how_members_connect: Minimum Capital Requirements for Operational Risk cites Basel III Post-Crisis Reforms and mandates the Standardized Approach; SOPE is the SAMA-implemented instrument referencing that requirement.

A defined calculation chain: Business Indicator -> Business Indicator Component -> combined with the Internal Loss Multiplier (built from the Loss Component and Standardized Approach Loss Data Set / Loss Event Type Classification) -> Operational Risk Capital.
Rules on Stress Testing cite BCBS principles and require Stress Testing feeding ICAAP, using scenario/sensitivity/reverse and top-down analysis, with operational risk as one tested dimension.
Pillar 3 Disclosure requirements consume the loss data set outputs, linking the capital-computation and public-disclosure obligations.

18.theme: Deposit account operating rules intersecting with AML/CTF customer due diligence and prudential reporting for deposit-taking institutions, including deposit-taking finance companies. Covers account types, KYC/beneficial-owner verification, dormancy/freezing, and asset-quality reporting.
how_members_connect: Accounts Operating Rules define and govern General, Deposit, and Term Deposit accounts and the sub-regimes for juristic persons, inactive/dormant accounts, and freezing/updating — all keyed to the General Account definition.

KYC links to CTF Due Diligence Measures and AML Due Diligence Measures; beneficial-owner identification/verification (incl. Awqaf) ties account onboarding to the AML and CTF Implementing Regulations under the Supervisory Authority.
Deposit Taking Finance Company (DTFC) is subject to prudential returns — Appendix A (capital to RWA), Appendix B (liquidity) — connecting account rules to reporting obligations.
Loan Review / Classification and Provisioning with Appendix C asset-quality classification sit alongside as SAMA-supervised credit-quality reporting for the same institutions.

19.theme: SAMA framework for managing problem loans: early identification, workout governance, viability analysis, and restructuring options for distressed exposures, anchored to credit-risk classification/provisioning rules under the Banking Control Law.
how_members_connect: An escalation chain: Early Warning Signals feed the Watch List, which routes exposures to the Workout Unit that builds the Workout Plan and monitors it via Restructuring KPIs and ongoing EWS.
NPL Strategy drives Portfolio Segmentation and Initial Viability Assessment, which invoke coverage metrics (LLCR, DSCR) and NPV analysis to test financial/business viability.

Restructuring/Workout Options cite the Banking Control Law and branch into short-term measures, long-term/permanent restructuring, and conditional loan forgiveness — the permitted regulatory outcomes.
Credit Risk Classification and Provisioning Rules govern how restructured/distressed exposures must be classified and provisioned, tying the workout process back to prudential obligations.

20.theme: Prudential and governance regime for foreign bank branches and agent banking arrangements in KSA, all subordinate to the Banking Control Law. Covers how a licensed foreign branch must be governed, funded and liquid, and how a principal bank may deploy banking agents while retaining regulatory responsibility.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the Banking Control Law is the enabling statute cited by both the FBB Regulations and the Agent Banking Regulation, which act as implementing rules with mandatory attachments (Return Form A, LCR/NSFR B, RWA/Funding D) as prescribed reporting obligations.

FBB Regulations chain governance and prudential duties onto the branch: corporate governance/risk management, the GM/CEO Senior Management Function, and liquidity requirements (LCR, NSFR, FR, CFP) that resolve into specific reporting attachments.

Agent Banking Regulation defines the principal Bank and its Banking Agent, allocating obligations: Fit & Proper assessment sits on the principal, while AML/CFT-KYC and Consumer Protection duties attach at the agent-facing customer interface.
Cross-regime flag: agent banking pulls in AML/CFT/KYC and Consumer Protection regimes — the principal bank remains accountable for agent conduct despite outsourcing the customer touchpoint.

21.theme: Liquidity and funding prudential regime for Islamic profit-sharing accounts and the broader ILAAP framework, addressing how PSIA (Mudarabah-based, non-guaranteed) balances are treated for LCR/NSFR and internal liquidity adequacy, plus supporting reporting on rates and loan-to-deposit ratios.
how_members_connect: PSIA Rules define the account and its Mudarabah/PERR-IRR mechanics, then feed the LCR/NSFR Prudential Requirements for PSIA — the defined term drives distinct prudential treatment because PSIA holders bear investment risk.

ILAAP Guidelines govern the ILAAP Process, which cross-references LCR/NSFR ratios, Pillar 2 liquidity drivers, stress-testing, CFP and Early Warning Indicators as an integrated internal assessment obligation.

Reporting guidelines (Interest Rates on Assets/Liabilities, LDR) supply the calculation inputs (weighted average rates, weighted denominator, A&L categories) that share data with the prudential ratios.
Concepts cluster by shared liquidity-metric dependency rather than strict hierarchy — LDR and LCR/NSFR are conceptually related monitoring measures.

22.theme: Basel-derived LCR and NSFR calculation mechanics and monitoring tools as adopted by SAMA, covering the numerator/denominator components and supplementary funding-concentration and currency-mismatch metrics.
how_members_connect: Authority chain: components cite the source BCBS LCR (Jan 2013) and NSFR (Oct 2014) documents plus SAMA circulars (BCS 771, Leverage Ratio 351000133367) as the standards SAMA transposes.

LCR side references the Stock of HQLA formula, Level 2 asset cap, and monitoring tools (funding concentration, significant counterparty, LCR by currency); NSFR side references ASF/RSF, interdependent assets/liabilities and off-balance-sheet exposures.
Derivative treatment links across the ratio: NSFR Derivative Assets/Liabilities share data and both cite the Leverage Ratio circular for their measurement basis.
Relationships are largely definitional/calculational cross-references — these are the technical building blocks that operationalize the prudential ratios in communities 20-21.

23.theme: Counterparty credit risk (SA-CCR) and credit valuation adjustment (CVA) capital framework, defining how banks compute derivative and SFT exposures and the associated CVA capital charge.
how_members_connect: SA-CCR is the anchor: it references the CCR Framework it implements and the components (EAD, Replacement Cost, Netting Set, NICA) that build the exposure calculation, with worked examples (SA-CCR Sample Portfolio) and the EAD Formula as illustrative detail.
Replacement Cost is elaborated by Netting Set, NICA and Standard Margin Agreements effects — collateral and netting arrangements directly reduce measured exposure.
The CVA Framework cross-references SA-CCR (exposure feeds CVA) and branches into BA-CVA (reduced and full versions) and SA-CVA delta/vega risk classes, with Eligible CVA Hedges recognized as offsets.
Master Netting Agreements for SFTs and the Market Risk Framework are referenced as adjacent regimes governing exposure aggregation and risk-class treatment.

24.theme: Internal control and technology-risk governance for finance companies: the cluster binds the three-lines control functions (compliance, internal audit, Shariah governance, code of conduct) to SAMA's IT, cyber, and business-continuity frameworks, plus the operational IT sub-disciplines they mandate.
how_members_connect: Control-function instruments (Compliance, Internal Audit, Shariah Governance, Code of Conduct) cross-reference each other, establishing that audit and compliance test conduct and Shariah adherence as enforceable governance obligations.

Internal Audit ties into the IT Governance Framework, extending audit scope to technology controls; the Framework in turn references the Cyber Security and Business Continuity Frameworks as the anchoring SAMA-issued standards.

Operational IT topics (change management, patching, development, testing, incident management, data backup) are subordinate practices that reference the Cyber Security and Business Continuity Frameworks — treat the Frameworks as the source of obligation and these as implementing detail.
IT Governance Maturity Model is a measurement companion to the Framework, not an independent obligation source.

25.theme: Core banking, payments, and consumer-finance supervision: the law-to-regulation hierarchy governing licensing, prudential/reporting duties, consumer protection, and credit information across banks, PSPs, and finance companies.
how_members_connect: Primary statutes (Banking Control Law, Finance Companies Control Law, Credit Information Law) sit at the top; implementation rules and implementing regulations (SAMA 1429, Payments Law reg SAMA 1430) operationalise them into supervisory, reporting, and licensing obligations.

The Payments Law implementing regulation is the hub for PSP duties — it references licensing, payment services, risk/compliance, complaints, and customer protection, defining who may operate and under what conduct obligations.

Model Consumer Finance Contract (SAMA 1611) draws multiple regimes together — Finance Companies Control Law, Credit Information Law, APR, early repayment, and consumer protection — making it a composite compliance reference for finance contracts.

Consumer Protection Principles and the payments regime's Customer Protection provisions are semantically aligned; note both terms coexist across regimes and should be scoped to the relevant instrument.

26.theme: The prescriptive APR calculation regime for consumer finance: the mandatory net-present-value method, SAMA's certified calculator, and the finance-company rules that set fee, credit-limit, term, and dispute constraints.
how_members_connect: Rules Governing Calculation of APR anchor the cluster, referencing the NPV method, the SAMA APR Calculator, and the enabling Finance Companies Control Law / Consumer Financing Regulations as the binding methodology.

The APR Calculator (Excel) plus its Certification Circular make SAMA's tool the authoritative computation — the method (NPV) and Annex 1 are semantically the same substantive rule expressed in different instruments.

Consumer Financing Regulations act as the umbrella, cross-referencing Maximum Credit Limit and Term Rules, Dispute Resolution Rules, Outsourcing Rules, and Licensed Credit Bureau — defining the surrounding compliance perimeter for financing.
The Article 83 / Article 9 fees clarification circular interprets the Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law, constraining what fees may enter the APR.

27.theme: AML/CTF and operating-conduct regime for exchange houses and money-service operations: KYC/CDD duties, suspicious-transaction and cross-border reporting, and account/secrecy rules anchored in the AML Law and FATF standards.
how_members_connect: The Exchange Houses Operating Procedures Guide is the central conduct instrument, referencing the AML Law, CDD, KYC, correspondent banking, cross-border cash transport, STR, and FATF as its obligation sources.
CDD and KYC are treated as linked defined concepts; STR feeds the Financial Investigations Unit, establishing the reporting obligation chain from detection to authority.

Rules Regulating Exchange Business (Decision 1730) is the licensing/operating framework, updated by the Cross-Border Cash Movement Data Requirement and Work Procedures updates — treat these as amendments to operating duties.

Account-related instruments (Current Account Template, Banking Accounts Rules, Data on Bank Accounts) reference the AML Law and Banking Secrecy, showing account onboarding and data-disclosure obligations sit within the same AML/secrecy tension.

28.theme: Market-risk capital under the Internal Models Approach (IMA): the eligibility, backtesting and P&L-attribution gateway a bank must pass to keep using internal models for trading-book capital under SAMA's Basel-aligned market-risk regime.
how_members_connect: IMA is the parent authorisation; ES Model, RFET, PLA Test and Backtesting are the referenced conditions a firm must satisfy to retain and calibrate model-based capital.

RFET operationalises the split between modellable and Non-Modellable Risk Factors (NMRF); NMRFs are capitalised separately via Stressed ES (SES), which then feeds the IMCC aggregate requirement alongside ES.

Backtesting compares Actual vs Hypothetical P&L and assigns Green/Amber/Red zones — an obligation whose outcome (Red) triggers loss of IMA eligibility; PLA compares Risk-Theoretical vs Hypothetical P&L using Spearman and Kolmogorov-Smirnov metrics as the pass/fail tests.
Liquidity Horizon scales both the ES model and the DRC (default risk) component, linking risk-factor tenor to the capital number.

29.theme: Counterparty credit risk and fund/equity exposure measurement: the hierarchy of approaches banks must apply to look through fund holdings, capitalise settlement risk, and observe the aggregate constraints under SAMA's Basel III adoption.
how_members_connect: Equity Investments in Funds sets a mandated cascade — Look-Through (LTA), then Mandate-Based (MBA), then Fall-Back (FBA) — determining how underlying exposures are risk-weighted; LTA/MBA reference the IRB Approach and carry Leverage Adjustment and CVA/CCR treatment.
Unsettled Transactions/Failed Trades and its Capital Treatment split obligations by settlement mechanism: DvP versus Non-DvP (free deliveries), the latter drawing IRB-style treatment.

Basel III Framework is the cited authority for CCR, Output Floor and Pillar 3; Output Floor constrains IRB-derived RWA and is disclosed via the Pillar 3 framework — a hierarchy linking measurement approach to aggregate floor and public disclosure.

30.theme: Minimum capital for counterparty credit risk (CCR) and credit valuation adjustment (CVA): the two-track (internal-model IMM and standardised SA-CVA) regime SAMA requires, including validation and disclosure templates.
how_members_connect: Minimum Capital Requirements for CCR and CVA is the governing provision referencing both the IMM and the CVA Framework as permitted calculation routes.
IMM eligibility is conditioned on Netting Set/Cross-Product Netting rules, Wrong-Way Risk, Stress Testing and Backtesting/Model Validation — obligations a firm must meet, subject to SAMA approval.

CVA Framework references SA-CVA, which drives Regulatory CVA Calculation via Delta/Vega sensitivities; SFT collateral haircut floors and disclosure templates (CCR5, CVA3) map the numbers to reporting.
SAMA is referenced as the approving/supervising authority for IMM and SA-CVA use.

31.theme: Leverage ratio and SA-CCR exposure measurement plus the output floor: the non-risk-based backstop and standardised counterparty exposure rules that constrain and aggregate a bank's RWA under SAMA's framework.
how_members_connect: SA-CCR (with PFE Add-on, Maturity Factor and Margin Period of Risk) is the mandated standardised method for derivative counterparty exposure, cited by both Derivative Exposures Treatment and the CCR/CVA minimum-capital rules.
The Leverage Ratio Exposure Measure aggregates derivative, SFT, off-balance-sheet (CCF) and written-credit-derivative exposures into the non-risk-based denominator.
The Output Floor (72.5% RWA) binds together RWA for credit, market, and CCR/CVA risk — capping the benefit of internal models by flooring total RWA against standardised outputs.
RWA for CCR and CVA cites the SAMA CCR and CVA minimum-capital provision, linking the exposure calculation back to the capital requirement it feeds.

32.theme: Prudential and conduct regime for licensed finance companies: licensing, capital/liquidity, governance, risk and compliance obligations, plus consumer-facing fee, APR and contract requirements. Covers what a finance company must satisfy to operate and how it must price and document consumer finance.
how_members_connect: The Implementing Regulation of the Finance Companies Control Law is the parent instrument, referencing licensing, capital adequacy/liquidity, corporate governance, risk management, compliance function, exposure limits and financing policies as subordinate obligations.

Consumer-conduct branch links Administrative Fees Regulatory Provisions and the Services Tariff Guide (fee ceilings/disclosure) to Consumer Finance Controls; Finance Contract Requirements incorporate the mandated APR Formula for cost-of-credit disclosure.
Financing Policies and Procedures bridge the prudential governance layer to the contract-level requirements, tying internal controls to enforceable customer documentation.
The two Tariff Guide entries are duplicates (semantically similar) and should be treated as one authority.

33.theme: Licensing and supervision of finance-support activities (notably debt collection) and adjacent BNPL/payments and AML governance obligations, sitting under the Finance Companies Control Law framework and its finance-lease dimension.
how_members_connect: Rules for Licensing Finance Support Activities is the anchor; the Amendment and the debt-collection circulars (outsourcing, cancellation of the licensing requirement) amend/reference it, showing an evolving licensing perimeter for collection operations.

The Implementing Regulations of the Finance Companies Control Law (with Finance Lease Law) is the parent authority cited by most members, including the promissory-note credit-card circular and the Raising BNPL Financing Ceiling circular that adjusts a BNPL product limit.
Governance and AML linkage: Compliance with Governance Principles and the Business Risk Assessment Guide for ML/TF/PF connect the licensing regime to enterprise-wide risk-assessment obligations.

Payments cross-regime edges: PSP licensing guidelines and the Payment Systems Oversight Framework relate conceptually via shared AML/governance expectations; note duplicate entries for the BRA Guide and Oversight Framework should be de-duplicated.

34.theme: Statutory supervision of banks' investment activity and money-changing business under the Banking Control Law and Central Bank Law, with cross-cutting AML/CTF, licensing, customer protection and outsourcing obligations.
how_members_connect: Banks Investment Rules cite the Banking Control Law and Central Bank Law as enabling authority and reference investment governance, risk management/monitoring, approval controls and investment policy as its operative requirements.

Rules Regulating Money Changing Business form a parallel licensed-activity regime, referencing the defined term Money Changer, licensing procedures, customer protection and third-party outsourcing controls.

AML/CTF is the shared cross-regime obligation: both the investment risk-monitoring provisions and the money-changing rules link to Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing, which cites the Anti-Money Laundering Law as its statutory base.

35.theme: Basel-aligned market-risk capital rules under the SAMA standardised approach (SMAR), specifically the Default Risk Capital charge and its treatment across securitisation and non-securitisation exposures.
how_members_connect: The Standardised Approach (Market Risk) is the umbrella methodology; the DRC Requirement and Residual Risk Add-On are its component charges feeding RWA for Market Risk under SMAR minimum capital requirements.
The DRC Requirement decomposes into DRC for Non-Securitisations, DRC for Securitisations (CTP) and (non-CTP), each computed using the Jump-to-Default risk measure and the Hedge Benefit Ratio.
Correlation Trading Portfolio is the defined scope for the CTP-specific DRC treatment, distinguishing it from ordinary securitisation exposures.

36.theme: SAMA's account-opening and operation regime for banks, centered on the umbrella 'Rules for Bank Accounts' and its account-type-specific annexes, integrating KYC/AML obligations and cross-referencing corporate-insolvency law.
how_members_connect: The 'Rules for Bank Accounts' is the parent instrument; each specialized regime (Government Entity, Non-resident Juristic Persons, WAMY, Liquidation/Restructuring, Correspondent) is subordinate and references it for baseline definitions and General Rules for Operation.
Chapter I: Definitions and the General Rules supply the shared defined terms and operational obligations applied across all account types.

AML/CFT obligations enter via the KYC Principle and AML/CFT Form, imposed on higher-risk openings (non-resident juristic persons, correspondent relationships) — note KYB-style due diligence on juristic customers.
Liquidation/Restructuring account rules cross-reference the Bankruptcy Law and Companies Law, tying account operation to insolvency and corporate-status triggers.

37.theme: SAMA's Financial Entities Ethical Red Teaming (F.E.E.R.) framework governing intelligence-led adversarial security testing of regulated financial entities, subordinate to the SAMA Cyber Security Framework.
how_members_connect: F.E.E.R. is the governing framework defining participant roles (Red, Blue, White, Green Teams) and their mandated deliverables.
Obligation chain runs to specific outputs: Red Teaming Provider produces the RTER, Blue Team produces the BTR, and White Team owns the Remediation Plan drawing on both reports.
Methodology terms (Cyber Kill Chain, Threat Intelligence, Penetration Testing) are defined-by F.E.E.R. and scope how testing must be conducted.
The Red Teaming Provider is anchored to the SAMA Cyber Security Framework, establishing F.E.E.R. as a subordinate/complementary regime within SAMA's cyber-supervision hierarchy.

38.theme: Basel SA-CCR counterparty credit-risk capital methodology as adopted by SAMA — the PFE add-on calculation for derivative exposures and the alternative Internal Models Method.
how_members_connect: The PFE Add-on is the aggregating provision that references the five asset-class add-ons (interest rate, FX, credit, equity, commodity).
Each add-on is built from shared computational inputs — Hedging Set, Effective Notional, Supervisory Factor and Maturity Factor — establishing a definitional dependency chain.
Maturity Factor is defined by reference to the Margin Period of Risk (MPOR), linking add-on calculation to margining assumptions.
IMM is the alternative approach, referencing Effective EPE and MPOR — flagging that a firm's method choice determines which parameters govern its capital calculation.

39.theme: The supervisory parameter set underpinning SA-CCR add-on calculations under SAMA's counterparty credit-risk rules, including the summary parameter table and worked examples.
how_members_connect: Effective Notional is the central computed input, derived from Adjusted Notional and the Supervisory Delta Adjustment, and feeds every asset-class add-on.
Supervisory Factor and Supervisory Correlation Parameters are regulator-prescribed values applied within each add-on and consolidated in Table 2: Summary of Supervisory Parameters.
Hedging Set defines the netting scope within which the parameters operate across the FX, commodity and interest-rate add-ons.
SA-CCR Sample Portfolio Examples reference the add-ons to illustrate correct application — useful as interpretive/worked guidance rather than a source of obligations.

40.theme: Account-opening rules for juristic (non-natural) persons under SAMA's Rules for Opening Bank Accounts, covering the differentiated KYB/documentation regimes applicable to distinct legal-entity categories (companies, foreign investors, awqaf, associations, foundations, diplomatic missions, and special-purpose accounts).
how_members_connect: The parent 'Rules for Opening Bank Accounts for Juristic Persons' is the governing instrument; each entity-type account (companies, escrow, embassies, endowments, foreign-investor residents, Hajj/Umrah, etc.) is a scoped sub-regime whose specific identification and documentation conditions the Rules reference.

Cross-references to external authorities set the licensing/registration precondition banks must verify: Private Associations and Private Foundations accounts depend on Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development oversight; Endowments and Bequests accounts depend on the General Authority for Awqaf.

For compliance decisions, each account type imposes a distinct customer-verification obligation — the correct CDD/KYB package turns on which sub-regime the applicant falls under, not a single generic standard.

41.theme: Basel-based minimum capital requirements for credit and counterparty credit risk (CCR), including central counterparty (CCP) exposures, as adopted in KSA through the SAMA Basel Framework.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: SAMA (issuer) and the SAMA Basel Framework sit above the substantive rule 'Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk'; the Guidance Note on Scope of Application and legacy Basel II Circular BCS 290 fix which entities and consolidation basis the framework binds.

'Minimum Capital Requirements for Credit Risk' is the hub that the CCR components elaborate — Effective EPE internal model, Cross-Product Netting, CCR in the Trading Book, and SFT haircut floors all reference it as their capital-calculation base.

CCP capital forms a nested obligation chain: Capital Requirements for CCP Exposures draws on Default Fund Exposure requirements, which in turn depend on the Hypothetical Capital Requirement (KCCP) computation.
Decision-relevance: these define how a bank must size regulatory capital against counterparty exposures; netting-recognition and haircut-floor conditions are limits/preconditions, not options.

42.theme: Credit risk classification and expected-credit-loss (ECL) provisioning for finance companies, aligning SAMA prudential classification with IFRS 9 staging and impairment.
how_members_connect: Legal anchor: Credit Risk Classification references the Finance Companies Control Law (the enabling statute) and IFRS 9 (the accounting standard whose ECL methodology it operationalises).

Concept chain: Stage 1/2/3 classification is driven by definitions of Default, Forbearance and Restructuring; Write-off relates to Default, and Restructuring is treated as a form of Forbearance affecting staging.
Governance and Credit Risk Management provisions impose oversight duties over ECL Provisioning — i.e., the board/management accountability layer sits on top of the IFRS 9 measurement obligation.
Decision-relevance: staging outcomes determine provisioning levels; misclassification of forborne/restructured exposures directly affects regulatory-provision adequacy.

43.theme: The Basel leverage-ratio framework's exposure-measure rules, focused on how derivatives, SFTs, written credit derivatives and CCR-related items are captured in the non-risk-based denominator.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the Leverage Ratio Framework governs the Leverage Ratio Exposure Measure, which decomposes into Derivative Exposures, SFT Exposures and their calculation methods.

Derivative-exposure treatment references the specific measurement components — Cash Variation Margin Treatment, Written Credit Derivatives Treatment, and Qualifying CCP status — that determine what may reduce or must inflate the exposure figure.
SFT exposure calculation depends on recognition of a Qualifying Master Netting Agreement and QCCP status, setting the conditions under which netting is permitted.
Risk-integrity conditions (Wrong-way Risk, CCR Stress Testing Program) constrain the exposure and internal-model treatment, so they act as qualifying limits rather than standalone capital rules.
